title: Protecting the ‘Privacy’ in Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: Lessons from Apple’s NeuralHash Detection Proposal and Google’s Privacy Sandbox
affiliations: and Irish Council for Civil Liberties

detail.title: Protecting the ‘Privacy’ in Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: Lessons from Apple’s NeuralHash Detection Proposal and Google’s Privacy Sandbox

keywords: Right to Respect for Private Life
Right to Protection of Personal Data

detail.abstract:
A report produced from a collaboration between Maria Helen Murphy (Maynooth University School of Law) and Kris Shrishak (Irish Council for Civil Liberties)

Privacy-Enhancing Technologies (PETs) are often presented as tools that enable the free flow of data while protecting personal information. In practice, however, PETs often fall short on their promise of safeguarding privacy without limiting data use. When privacy is reduced to a narrow conception of confidentiality, the tools marketed to enhance privacy risk undermining protection and entrenching existing concentrations of power. Drawing on two high-profile attempts at real-world deployment that were ultimately discontinued, this report shows how current approaches to PETs can obscure important risks, and that PETs must be understood as one component of a wider, rights-based governance framework rather than a technical fix for privacy problems. Crucially, broad engagement with diverse interdisciplinary stakeholders is an essential part of the process. In a time of legislative flux, where ‘simplification’ in pursuit of innovation is prominent in policy discussions, the limitations of PETs as a catch-all ‘solution’ must be accurately understood. This is especially the case as ongoing debates on the very ‘notion of personal data’, as reflected in the EU Digital Omnibus proposals, have the potential to further emphasise technical protections based on concepts of identifiability at the expense of full consideration of privacy harms.

title: Institutional Licensing Continuity and Expatriate Workforce Oversight in Regulated Organizations in Uganda

detail.title: Institutional Licensing Continuity and Expatriate Workforce Oversight in Regulated Organizations in Uganda
detail.abstract: This study investigates how institutional licensing continuity and expatriate workforce oversight influence compliance effectiveness and organizational performance in regulated organizations in Uganda, within a context characterized by regulatory fragmentation and administrative complexity. Despite the critical importance of compliance in highly regulated sectors, existing research has largely examined licensing systems, expatriate workforce management, and digital compliance tools in isolation, with limited attention to their interdependence in emerging economies. Grounded in Institutional Theory, the Resource-Based View (RBV), and Compliance Theory, the study adopts a conceptual research design supported by a structured and systematic review of scholarly literature, institutional reports, and regulatory frameworks. The analysis focuses on how organizations navigate multi-agency regulatory requirements, including licensing, registration, and immigration compliance, and how internal capabilities shape compliance outcomes. The findings reveal that institutional licensing continuity is a fundamental determinant of organizational legitimacy and operational stability, while inadequate expatriate workforce oversight significantly increases legal, financial, and operational risk. The study further demonstrates a strong interdependence between these compliance domains, particularly where immigration approvals depend on valid organizational licensing. Integrated digital systems, such as Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Human Resource Information Systems (HRIS), are identified as critical enabling and mediating mechanisms that enhance compliance effectiveness through automation, real-time monitoring, and centralized data.

title: Auditing Risks of Platforms in use under the DSA: A Case for user-side Observability
affiliations: Sciences Po Paris

detail.title: Auditing Risks of Platforms in use under the DSA: A Case for user-side Observability
detail.abstract: The Digital Services Act (DSA) establishes a multi-layered transparency and accountability regime for very large online platforms, relying primarily on platform selfreporting, researcher access to data, and periodic audits. This paper argues that these instruments suffer from epistemic limitations that are symptoms of an evidence architecture in which the data available for regulatory scrutiny is produced, curated, and formatted by the entities that are meant to be governed by the scrutiny. The paper shows that even bottom-up alternatives, such as data donation, which change who initiates data collection, reproduce the same gaps because the data still originates within the platform's infrastructure. Drawing on recent research in algorithmic auditing, participatory methods, and ecological momentary assessment, the paper proposes userside observability as a complementary evidentiary approach that captures platform risks at the point of user encounter rather than at the point of platform design. The legal and methodological conditions under which such evidence could be admitted into DSA enforcement proceedings, including its relationship to the Article 40 researcher access framework, are discussed.

title: Timing the Valve: How Does Intellectual Property Impact on Early Market Entry for mRNA Vaccines in Australia to Promote Vaccine Equity?
affiliations: University of Tasmania and TC Beirne School of Law, University of Queensland

detail.title: Timing the Valve: How Does Intellectual Property Impact on Early Market Entry for mRNA Vaccines in Australia to Promote Vaccine Equity?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not Applicable

detail.abstract: Much has been written about the potential for intellectual property to act as a barrier to access to medicines and vaccines for the most disadvantaged members of the global community (Tenni et al., 2022; Islam et al., 2019). The COVID experience provides a salutary lesson on the global failure to distribute vaccines equitably (Borges et al., 2022). The central focus of this chapter in on the need for improved vaccine equity, as defined by the US-based Centers for Disease Control: “when everyone, regardless of socioeconomic status, race, ethnicity, geographic location, or other determinants of health, has a fair and just opportunity to be vaccinated”. (Centres for Disease Control, 2024). We first discuss existing flexibilities in national and international intellectual property laws that may assist in alleviating concerns about lack of vaccine equity. We then consider the intellectual property landscape for a small group of relevant vaccines that serve as case studies for our analysis and assess whether any of the available flexibilities may be applicable. We explain in Part 1 that a number of relevant flexibilities exist in the Australian Patents Act 1990 (Cth) (Patents Act) which are compliant with international obligations. However, equivalent flexibilities do not exist for other forms of intellectual property, particularly the exclusivity that is provided by national agencies tasked with granting approvals for marketing of vaccine products for the use of clinical trials and other data submitted to them (which we refer to as hereafter regulatory data). This is problematic if it means that follow-on vaccine developers have to wait for expiry of the exclusivity period or undertake the costly and lengthy process of generating their own data. In Part 2, we ask the following question: when a first-in-class mRNA vaccine is provisionally or fully approved by the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) for inclusion on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG), what actually determines the earliest lawful entry of a follow-on product? In addressing this question, we analyse patent and ARTG databases for the most commonly used platform technology for mRNA vaccine delivery to determine whether patents or regulatory data exclusivity create a binding “timing valve” for follow-on products. We then test whether any of the permissible flexibilities discussed in Part 1 could  alleviate timing valve limitations. We conclude that it would be unwise to rely solely on these flexibilities and that other strategies will be needed to ensure that Australia can meet its obligations with regard to vaccine equity

title: Secure and Sustainable Logistics: Integrating Cybersecurity Risk Management into Circular Supply Chain Models
affiliations: Hellenic Open University, University of Piraeus and Hellenic Open University

detail.title: Secure and Sustainable Logistics: Integrating Cybersecurity Risk Management into Circular Supply Chain Models

declarations.funderStatement: The research conducted in this paper was triggered by the authors’ involvement in the projects: ‘Collaborative, Multi-modal and Agile Professional Cybersecurity Training Program for a Skilled Workforce In the European Digital Single Market and Industries’ (CyberSecPro) GA No 101083594 and "AIDriven Threat Detection and VR Cyber Defense" (DomeSentinel), CyberSecDome (GA No 101120779) Open Call-Round#1. The views expressed in this paper represent only the views of the authors and not of the European Union nor of the partners in the above-mentioned projects.

detail.abstract: Supply chains are being redesigned under persistent pressure to reduce emissions, recover materials, and improve resource efficiency. Reverse logistics flows, remanufacturing cycles, and carbon-aware routing mechanisms are gradually embedded into everyday operations. Yet these processes no longer function without a dense digital layer. Routing engines, traceability platforms, cloud-based coordination services and automated analytics engines now mediate almost every sustainability-related decision. This dependence introduces a structural tension. The same infrastructure that enables environmental optimization also enlarges the attack surface of logistics networks. A corrupted routing parameter, a delayed synchronization process, or manipulated traceability records may not only interrupt operations but also silently distort sustainability metrics. Still, most evaluation models treat environmental performance and cybersecurity exposure as unrelated assessment domains. This study proposes a Secure and Sustainable Logistics Framework that treats cyber-resilience as an internal performance variable rather than as an external safeguard. Instead of appending a risk indicator to a sustainability dashboard, cybersecurity metrics are mathematically embedded into circular supply chain evaluation. Energy intensity, emissions per transport unit, recovery rates, and traceability accuracy are evaluated jointly with vulnerability exposure, incident likelihood, detection capability, and recovery readiness. To operationalize this interaction, we formulate the Secure Sustainability Index (SSI), a composite construct that captures sustainability performance under residual cyber-risk conditions. SSI is designed and implemented for controlled experimentation rather than large-scale deployment. In the simulation environment, cyber events-such as data tampering or service disruption-are mapped to measurable logistics consequences, including extended transport distances, higher fuel consumption, and temporary degradation of recovery efficiency. In addition, repeated disturbance scenarios where included that reveal a non-trivial pattern: systems optimized primarily for environmental performance exhibit higher volatility when cyber preparedness is limited. Configurations that distribute investment more evenly across digital security and sustainability indicators demonstrate lower drawdowns and faster stabilization. The study therefore positions cybersecurity not as a parallel compliance requirement, but as a conditioning variable for sustainable logistics stability.

title: Strengthening Data Integrity In U.S. Economic Reporting Systems: The Role Of Structured Governance And Regulatory Compliance Framework

detail.title: Strengthening Data Integrity In U.S. Economic Reporting Systems: The Role Of Structured Governance And Regulatory Compliance Framework
detail.abstract: This study examines how structured governance and regulatory compliance frameworks enhance data integrity in U.S. economic reporting systems and strengthen regulatory oversight. As economic reporting increasingly relies on complex digital infrastructures, ensuring the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of data has become a critical challenge for organizations, regulators, and policymakers. Drawing on a qualitative, conceptual research design, this study synthesizes existing literature from accounting, information systems, and regulatory practice to analyze the roles of governance frameworks, enterprise systems, and emerging technologies in supporting data integrity. The findings indicate that while regulatory frameworks such as the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, oversight by the Securities and Exchange Commission, and standards under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles have significantly improved accountability and transparency, persistent challenges remain. These include data fragmentation, inconsistent governance practices, system integration limitations, and evolving technological risks. The study further demonstrates that enterprise systems, particularly ERP platforms, alongside emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, and XBRL, enhance reporting efficiency and accuracy but are insufficient in isolation. A key contribution of this research is the development of a conceptual framework that integrates structured governance, regulatory compliance, and technological capabilities to explain their collective impact on data integrity and regulatory oversight. The analysis highlights the interdependent nature of these elements and emphasizes the need for a systemsbased approach to economic reporting. The study concludes by proposing practical recommendations for strengthening data governance, improving system integration.

title: Ownership Without Control: Digital Lock-In and the Emergence of Conditional Ownership in Technological Economies

detail.title: Ownership Without Control: Digital Lock-In and the Emergence of Conditional Ownership in Technological Economies
detail.abstract: Technological products increasingly combine physical ownership with embedded digital systems that remain under manufacturer control. This development raises important questions regarding the evolving relationship between ownership, institutional authority, and user autonomy. While consumers may legally purchase and possess technologically advanced products, critical operational functions are often governed by proprietary software, diagnostic systems, and restricted component ecosystems. As a result, manufacturers may retain significant post-sale influence over the functionality, modification, and repair of products (Kohtala, 2017; Perzanowski & Schultz, 2016). This paper examines how digital technological architectures enable new forms of institutional control that subtly reshape traditional understandings of property rights. Using a publicly documented case involving the attempted independent rebuild of a modern hybrid vehicle as an illustrative example, the paper explores how software lock-in, diagnostic gatekeeping, and restricted component access can limit operational autonomy despite formal ownership. The analysis situates these developments within broader discussions of technological governance, corporate strategy, and leadership responsibility (Srnicek, 2017; Zuboff, 2019). The paper argues that digital integration allows organisations to exercise forms of post-sale digital authority, potentially transforming ownership from a condition of control into one of conditional access. The study contributes to emerging debates concerning right-to-repair movements, technological governance, and the ethical responsibilities of leadership in technologically mediated economies. It proposes a conceptual framework explaining how technological capabilities, strategic corporate choices, and digital control mechanisms interact to redefine the boundaries between ownership and institutional authority, contributing to the emergence of what may be described as conditional ownership regimes in technologically integrated products. Understanding this transformation is increasingly important as societies rely on products whose functionality depends on digitally controlled ecosystems.

title: ERP Integration With Immigration Compliance Monitoring In The United States

detail.title: ERP Integration With Immigration Compliance Monitoring In The United States
detail.abstract: The increasing globalization of the workforce has intensified the complexity of immigration compliance, particularly within the United States, where organizations must adhere to strict regulatory requirements such as Form I-9 and E-Verify. Traditional compliance approaches, often characterized by manual processes and fragmented systems, are increasingly inadequate in managing these demands. This study examines how Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems, specifically SAP and Oracle platforms, can be integrated with immigration compliance monitoring to enhance regulatory adherence, operational efficiency, and risk management. Adopting a qualitative research design based on secondary data analysis, the study draws on academic literature, government publications, industry reports, and ERP system documentation. A comprehensive literature review is conducted to synthesize existing knowledge on ERP systems, compliance management, and digital transformation, while identifying gaps in the integration of ERP with immigration compliance. The study further develops a conceptual framework grounded in Enterprise Systems Integration Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to explain how ERP systems facilitate compliance processes. The analysis, conducted using thematic analysis, reveals that ERP systems significantly improve immigration compliance monitoring by centralizing data, automating workflows, enhancing audit readiness, and enabling proactive risk management through analytics and real-time monitoring. In addition, the study provides practical recommendations for organizations, including integrating compliance into ERP workflows, adopting automation and AI-driven analytics, strengthening data governance, and ensuring continuous system updates to reflect regulatory changes.

title: Multi-Sided Platforms and Non-Adoption as Strategy

detail.title: Multi-Sided Platforms and Non-Adoption as Strategy

detail.abstract: In large organizations and multi-sided platform environments, decisions regarding AI adoption are increasingly delayed or avoided altogether. This paper reframes non-adoption not as resistance or conservatism, but as a rational strategic response to unresolved decision boundaries. As responsibility fragments across multiple actors-platform providers, vendors, regulators, and users-commitment to irreversible decisions becomes economically and organizationally risky. Drawing on platform strategy and governance dynamics, this paper identifies how decision deadlocks emerge and why waiting becomes a dominant strategy, highlighting the absence of decision infrastructure as the structural underlying condition.

title: The Authorization Threshold: Defining the Standard for Governance in AI Systems

detail.title: The Authorization Threshold: Defining the Standard for Governance in AI Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of FERZ, Inc., a company developing deterministic AI governance infrastructure. The concepts presented in this paper are consistent with the author’s research and professional work in this area. The paper is intended as a general theoretical and technical framework and does not evaluate specific commercial products.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental subjects. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and was not supported by external funding.

detail.abstract:
The resurgence of AI systems capable of initiating actions across institutional and regulatory domains has intensified the need for governance frameworks that extend beyond monitoring, alignment, and post hoc auditability. This paper argues that prevailing approaches to AI governance remain procedural in nature, focusing on capabilities such as observability, control mechanisms, and policy enforcement, rather than on the conditions required for governance to exist.

We propose the concept of an authorization threshold, defined as the point at which an action qualifies as governed: when its authorization can be established prior to execution under explicit, evaluable constraints and independently verified. Governance, in this formulation, is not a property of systems but of individual decisions made within a defined context.

To formalize this standard, the paper introduces the Canonical Action Frame, specifying the elements required to represent a governable action, and distinguishes between interpretive (judgment-based) systems and authorization (derivation-based) systems. It further develops a foundational distinction between evidence—which explains decisions after the fact—and proof, which constrains the space of permissible decisions before execution.

A central contribution is the identification of the constraint representation layer, the transformation of human-readable policy into canonical, machine-evaluable constraints, as the necessary condition for proof-capable governance. Building on this, the paper defines seven conditions of governance validity and five dimensions of governance completeness, including constraint completeness, semantic precision, policy binding, temporal binding, and independent replayability.

The paper concludes by specifying the structure of a proof-grade authorization artifact and proposing a testable standard for determining whether an AI-driven action has been governed. The framework provides a basis for evaluating governance claims, distinguishing governance-capable architectures from governance-adjacent systems, and advancing AI governance from interpretive oversight to formal authorization.

title: UK Data Protection Post-Brexit: The Evolving Landscape

detail.title: UK Data Protection Post-Brexit: The Evolving Landscape

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Research Paper No.3/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Cambridge Faculty of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Post-Brexit, the UK has clearly shifted to a more business and government-friendly data protection approach. Nevertheless, although wider changes have eliminated data protection as a fundamental right and deprived the UK GDPR of primacy vis-à-vis exemptions from the regime, the specific substantive reforms of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 are modest. Although limitations on automated individual decision-making rights do go further, almost all its substantive changes merely gloss prior law or could have found justification within the UK (and EU) GDPR's restrictions clause. Of more significance is the attempt, partly on the back of DUAA itself, to further and entrench a very limited and selective approach to regulatory enforcement. This approach seriously diverges not only from the exacting standards of the Court of Justice of the EU but also from the EU's practical norm. For example, whereas the EU issued 1,396 data protection fines of €1,254m or around £1,062m in 2024, the 2024/25 ICO figures are only 2 and around £4m respectively. Given that the UK GDPR's legal enforcement duties also remain largely intact, the extent to which this attempt at limitation will succeed remains uncertain. It should nevertheless lead to some questioning of whether UK data protection regulatory supervision is truly grounded in a rule of law which systematically safeguards data subjects' rights.

detail.abstract: User experience (UX) design has become an essential component of modern digital workplaces, influencing how employees interact with organizational systems and tools. As workplaces increasingly rely on digital platforms for communication, task management, and administrative processes, the quality of interface design plays a significant role in employee efficiency and productivity. This study examines the relationship between UX design and employee productivity through a review of existing academic literature. The research analyzes five scholarly studies focusing on visual ergonomics, user-centered design, usability testing, and UX optimization in workplace applications such as HR systems, attendance platforms, and digital collaboration tools. Findings from the literature indicate that effective UX design contributes to reduced human errors, faster task completion, improved system usability, and higher employee satisfaction. Additionally, user-centered interfaces support better learning outcomes and smoother administrative workflows. However, challenges remain in measuring productivity outcomes and generalizing findings across industries. Overall, the study highlights that investing in well-designed UX systems can significantly enhance workplace efficiency and employee performance in modern organizations.

title: Accountability Protocol: Decision, Exception, Responsibility

detail.title: Accountability Protocol: Decision, Exception, Responsibility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human subjects, participants, or identifiable personal data; therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in organizational and societal decision processes, failures increasingly arise not from technical malfunction but from unresolved boundaries of authority, exception response, and accountability. As AI-mediated decisions spread across organizations, accountability is often addressed through legal liability, ethics guidelines, or ad hoc managerial responses. This paper argues that such approaches fail to capture a deeper structural problem: accountability collapses when decision authority, exception response, and responsibility are not coherently aligned. We conceptualize accountability as a protocol rather than a role or rule, and examine how responsibility becomes displaced onto individuals or functions when decision boundaries are undefined. The paper demonstrates why existing organizational roles cannot absorb this burden and why accountability must be designed as part of decision infrastructure. This paper does not advocate technological restraint, but seeks to clarify the structural conditions under which accountability protocols become necessary.

title: Nonstandard Errors in AI Agents
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: Nonstandard Errors in AI Agents
detail.abstract: We study whether state-of-the-art AI coding agents, given the same data and research question, produce the same empirical results. Deploying 150 autonomous Claude Code agents to independently test six hypotheses about market quality trends in NYSE TAQ data for SPY (2015-2024), we find that AI agents exhibit sizable nonstandard errors (NSEs), that is, uncertainty from agent-to-agent variation in analytical choices, analogous to those documented among human researchers. AI agents diverge substantially on measure choice (e.g., autocorrelation vs. variance ratio, dollar vs. share volume). Different model families (Sonnet 4.6 vs. Opus 4.6) exhibit stable "empirical styles," reflecting systematic differences in methodological preferences. In a three-stage feedback protocol, AI peer review (written critiques) has minimal effect on dispersion, whereas exposure to top-rated exemplar papers reduces the interquartile range of estimates by 80-99% within converging measure families. Convergence occurs both through within-family estimation tightening and through agents switching measure families entirely. These findings have implications for the growing use of AI in automated policy evaluation and empirical research.

title: When Secondary Markets Go Democratic: Information, Learning, and Risk Allocation in Peer-to-Peer Lending Platforms
affiliations: , University of Warwick - Warwick Business School, University of Warwick and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: When Secondary Markets Go Democratic: Information, Learning, and Risk Allocation in Peer-to-Peer Lending Platforms
detail.abstract: Peer-to-peer (P2P) lending platforms have introduced secondary markets to improve liquidity and facilitate the resale of existing loans, yet many such markets have remained fragile and were ultimately discontinued. We study how secondary markets embedded in P2P lending platforms affect borrower participation, lender behavior, and market outcomes in decentralized environments without professional intermediaries to govern information disclosure or resale. We develop a model in which lenders trade loans under asymmetric information and learn about resale quality through market participation. The model shows that secondary markets create an ex ante resale option that relaxes funding constraints and attracts riskier borrowers, but also generate adverse selection that erodes liquidity over time as lenders update their beliefs from realized prices and repayment outcomes. We test the model using a quasi-natural experiment based on the introduction of a secondary market on a large Chinese P2P platform, using a comparable platform without resale as the control. Consistent with the model, we find that secondarymarket availability initially shifts funding toward higher-risk borrowers, while lenders who gain direct resale experience subsequently rebalance toward safer loans in the primary market. Our findings highlight a central tension in decentralized credit markets: the same resale mechanism that expands credit access can also generate the endogenous fragility that limits its long-run viability.

reference: USAEE Working Paper No. 26-665
title: Consumers' Preferences for Domestic Lithium Content in Electric Vehicles: A U.S. Discrete Choice Experiment
affiliations: Missouri University of Science and Technology, Missouri University of Science and Technology and Department of Economics, Applied Statistics, and International Business, New Mexico State University

detail.title: Consumers' Preferences for Domestic Lithium Content in Electric Vehicles: A U.S. Discrete Choice Experiment

publicationDetails.journalName: United States Association for Energy Economics (USAEE) & International Association for Energy Economics (IAEE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Despite substantial research on consumer preferences for electric vehicle (EV) performance, limited studies explicitly model preferences for domestic sourcing of battery minerals. We administer a discrete choice experiment to a nationally representative online sample of 1,200 U.S. respondents, incorporating the location of lithium mining and refining as key attributes. We randomly assign respondents to one of four information conditions: environmental impacts of lithium mining, emissions from refining, economic benefits of mining, or a control group. Mixed logit results reveal measurable but heterogeneous willingness to pay (WTP) for domestic sourcing. In the full sample, respondents are willing to pay approximately $29 per percentage-point increase in domestically mined lithium and $1,613 for domestic refining. Respondents exposed to positive information about economic benefits of mining are willing to pay $58 per percentage-point increase in domestic mining and $2,225 for domestic refining, whereas the control group does not exhibit a statistically significant valuation for these sourcing attributes. Respondents exposed to negative information about lithium refining show WTP of $24 and $1,608, respectively. These results suggest that information framing shapes preferences: positive information increases WTP for domestic sourcing, and negative information lowers but does not reverse preference for domestic sourcing. The findings highlight the importance of supply-chain transparency and informational context in shaping EV consumer preferences.

title: Ethical Nudging
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: Ethical Nudging
detail.abstract: All over the world, governments are using nudges as regulatory tools. Is this ethical? When? Much of the answer depends on whether nudges promote or instead undermine welfare, autonomy, and dignity. Many nudges, and those that deserve support, promote some or all of those ideals, and undermine none of them. If welfare is our guide, much nudging is actually required on ethical grounds, even if it comes from government. If autonomy is our guide, much nudging is also required on ethical grounds, in part because some nudges actually promote autonomy, in part because some nudges enable people to devote their limited time and attention to their most important concerns. Finally, nudges should not, and need not, compromise individual dignity, which many nudges actually promote. There is, however, a risk that some nudges might count as manipulation, as in the case of "dark patterns"; an emphasis on welfare, autonomy, and dignity helps to show how to avoid that risk.

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW - Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No.25-064

detail.abstract: We study the design of climate policy for hard-to-abate sectors, focusing on global aviation. We build a spatial equilibrium model that links ticket booking data, the global airline network, and climate regulated airlines’ choices in imperfectly competitive air transport markets. We find that sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) quotas out perform carbon pricing, delivering equal emissions cuts at 46–66% of the welfare cost. Ignoring market structure understates the cost of price-based Pigouvian instruments when fuel-capital substitution is limited. SAF quotas are more robust to regulatory scope, cause less carbon leakage, and—when layered with existing carbon pricing— increase abatement while lowering welfare cost. Relying on carbon offsets risks locking in fossil jet fuel, whereas cost-effective in-sector abatement hinges on substantial SAF uptake.

title: Celestial Origins of Egyptian Religion: An Asterism-Based Hypothesis on the Iconography of the Eye of Horus

detail.title: Celestial Origins of Egyptian Religion: An Asterism-Based Hypothesis on the Iconography of the Eye of Horus
detail.abstract: This paper posits a foundational celestial origin for the ancient Egyptian religious system, arguing that its core mythologies are derived from the pareidolic interpretation of a singular, dynamic stellar narrative. Centered on the Eye of Horus, the research demonstrates that this iconic symbol is not a static asterism but the central feature of a celestial saga whose nightly transit corresponds to a complete mythological cycle. This narrative sequentially reveals the stellar identities of key deities through the asterism's perceived transformations: first, the violent 'Hand of Seth' manifests during the Eye's initial wounding at the horizon; this is followed immediately by the integrated form of a lamenting 'Isis', whose own celestial body constitutes part of the injured Eye. Subsequently, the intervention of 'Thoth' facilitates its restoration during its ascent, and its culmination as the 'White Crown' at the celestial zenith symbolizes divine authority. The saga concludes with the asterism's rotational shift upon setting, which reconfigures it into the bovine form of 'Hathor', the ultimate protector of the perfected Eye. The hypothesis is substantiated by astronomical software simulations (Stellarium) and corroborated by direct iconographic and textual correspondences in foundational Egyptian religious texts, including the Pyramid and Coffin Texts. This study concludes that the interconnected myths surrounding these deities were not developed in isolation but were inspired by a unifying celestial template, the discovery of which provides a new paradigm for understanding the stellar genesis of ancient Egyptian religion.

title: From Compliance to Competence: Regime Selection as a Microfoundation for Prosocial Boosting

detail.title: From Compliance to Competence: Regime Selection as a Microfoundation for Prosocial Boosting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable (theoretical study).
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Standard preference-based models predict that prosocial behavior should become more frequent as costs fall. Yet agents who sustain substantial charitable commitments routinely overlook nearly costless everyday acts-holding a door, yielding a seat, picking up litter. Existing accounts attribute this gap to intrinsic effort aversion: agents lack sufficient motivation. We argue that the source lies not in a deficit of motivation but in a failure of representation. Everyday prosocial costs are simultaneously small in magnitude, heterogeneous in composition, and non-monetary in form. Their interaction generates a paradox: composition becomes decisive at precisely the magnitudes that deprive the agent of cognitive resources to represent it. We develop a regime-selection framework that formalizes this failure. A regime, as we define it, is not a utility function but the governing structure that determines which trade-offs enter the decision process-shifting the analytical unit from quantitative variation within a fixed evaluative frame to qualitative transition between frames. The framework distinguishes two representational states-one that parses cost composition against idiosyncratic preference weights, one that registers only aggregate magnitude-and models transition between them as a stochastic threshold problem. This structure identifies compositional advantage-the possibility that certain cost compositions are cheaper in utility terms even at fixed objective total magnitude-as a latent incentive present in the environment prior to any intervention. We ground the framework against the standard rational-inattention benchmark, then analyze how recognition of compositional structure and cumulative experience interact to produce durable or self-defeating cognitive change depending on initial conditions. The resulting dynamics provide a microfoundation for boosting (Hertwig and Grüne-Yanoff, 2017)-the cultivation of decision-making competence rather than the steering of behavior through environmental design-specifying what competence consists of, when it changes, and how its effects persist. The framework redefines successful intervention from compliance to competence, and its measure from increased prosocial frequency to prosocial flexibility-the capacity for informed acceptance and informed refusal.

title: Learning to Fuse Aspect-Level LLM Annotations for Low-Quality Ordinal Sentiment Supervision

detail.title: Learning to Fuse Aspect-Level LLM Annotations for Low-Quality Ordinal Sentiment Supervision
detail.abstract: Subjective text classification increasingly relies on imperfect supervision that is itself a noisy fusion of heterogeneous signals—user ratings, crowd labels, and foundation-model annotations. In domains where narratives encode multi-criterion trade-offs, collapsing evidence into a single holistic class yields diffuse confidence, unstable targets, and limited utility for uncertainty-based triage. We examine this setting in patient medication reviews, where platform ratings reflect heterogeneous utilities and rubric-guided holistic large language model (LLM) sentiment labeling exhibits persistently high uncertainty under a five-class ordinal scale. We recast supervision construction as an explicit multi-view fusion problem. Using gpt-4o-mini as a foundation-model view extractor, we elicit four clinically interpretable aspect views—efficacy, safety, burden, and cost—each labeled on a three-class polarity scale (negative, neutral, positive), alongside a holistic five-class confidence vector. We then learn non-negative aspect importance weights via multi-task transformer training and fuse aspect outputs into (i) five-class hard supervision through weighted aggregation and (ii) three-class soft targets through weighted vote distributions, yielding supervision that is robust to incomplete evidence (unmentioned aspects) and cross-aspect conflicts. On 102,061 deduplicated Drugs.com reviews, aspect-derived supervision improves downstream learnability across classical, neural, and transformer probes. ALBERT fine-tuned on aspect-derived hard labels achieves weighted F1=0.756, outperforming rating-derived supervision (0.651) and holistic LLM labels (0.674). These findings support an information-fusion principle for low-quality subjective supervision: extracting structured subdecisions aligned to textual evidence and learning an explicit aggregation rule yields more stable and learnable targets than single-shot holistic labeling.

title: A Harmonized Multi-Country Assessment of the Economic Costs of Road Traffic Injuries
affiliations: World Bank and World Bank

detail.title: A Harmonized Multi-Country Assessment of the Economic Costs of Road Traffic Injuries
detail.abstract: Road traffic injuries impose substantial socioeconomic losses on individuals, households, and national economies across diverse income levels. These losses arise from medical treatment, reduced productivity, property damage, and the wider welfare impacts associated with diminished quality of life. Although global estimates suggest that road crash costs account for between two and five percent of gross domestic product, many developing countries lack the systematic data and methodological consistency required to generate reliable national estimates. Recent analytical work supported by the World Bank seeks to address these gaps by applying a harmonized framework to estimate the economic and welfare burden of road traffic injuries across diverse settings.This paper synthesizes findings from costing studies conducted in Ecuador, Brazil, Saudi Arabia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. Each study employed a similar methodological framework, combining cost-of-illness estimates of medical, administrative, and property damage costs with human capital-based productivity losses and willingness-to-pay-based valuations of intangible human costs. Country-level analyses indicate that the combined welfare and economic burden of road traffic injuries is equivalent to approximately 3% of GDP in Saudi Arabia and up to 5% in Latin American countries. Across study settings, human costs accounted for nearly 80% of total losses, while medical costs accounted for less than 3%.The findings underscore the predominance of non-fatal injury burden, the sensitivity of estimates to data limitations, and the need for improved national surveillance systems. The evidence highlights the substantial economic gains achievable through targeted road safety investments and supports stronger integration of cost data into policy and planning processes.

title: HAR Inference for Quantile Regression in Time Series
affiliations: and Universidad de Tarapacá

detail.title: HAR Inference for Quantile Regression in Time Series
detail.abstract: Robust inference in time series quantile regression (QR) poses greater challenges than in conditional mean regression because of finite sample uncertainties arising from two nonparametric components of the asymptotic variance estimator: the conditional QR error density in the Hessian matrix and the long-run variance (LRV) of the nonsmooth QR score process. In this paper, we develop a novel QR heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation robust (HAR) inference procedure that integrates an alternative asymptotic inference with an MCMC-based estimator of the inverse QR Hessian. This combination allows us to bypass the kernel-based estimation of the conditional QR density and yields more accurate fixed-smoothing asymptotic approximation for the QR Wald statistic. Monte Carlo simulations show that the proposed QR-HAR inference delivers favorable finite sample size control and power compared to existing QR inference in time series. Notably, our QR-HAR inference framework not only applies to existing kernel and orthonormal series (OS) LRV estimators, it also incorporates tuning-parameter-free self-normalized inference without recursive QR parameter estimation.

detail.abstract: Hybrid threats encompass a range of hostile activities aimed at achieving geopolitical objectives, including cyberattacks, infrastructure sabotage, espionage, economic and political coercion, disinformation, and other forms of hybrid warfare. We construct a Geopolitical Hybrid Threat (GHT) index based on newspaper coverage of these activities. The index surges from the mid-2010s, surpassing the high levels observed during the late Cold War. Using a narrative instrument in a vector autoregression, we find that hybrid threat shocks suppress aggregate demand by raising uncertainty, reducing confidence, and tightening financial conditions, while triggering policy responses in the form of increased defense spending and monetary easing.

detail.abstract: Technology is not neutral with respect to the distribution of power. This claim, implicit in Ellul [1954], operationalised by Winner [1980], and stated as a counterthesis to instrumentalism by Feenberg [1991, 1999], has never been derived as a structural law. We show that from the Principle of Technological Non-Neutrality a law follows with logical necessity: the Law of Technological Power Displacement. The law states that technology systematically and irreversibly displaces power from the citizen space toward the public-corporate apparatus, automatically, invisibly, and independently of any agent's intentions. Three mechanisms drive this result: relational disorder generated by technological deployment, autocatalytic expansion of the regulatory apparatus, and endogenous decay of democratic restoration capacity through two channels, growing power asymmetry and epistemic captivity of the regulator. We formalise these mechanisms through three coupled diferential equations and prove the central theorem by a sign argument requiring no parametric assumptions. A named corollary formalises the automatic coup: the constitutional order is not overthrown by any deliberate political actor but eroded through individually unremarkable technical determinations until the democratic equilibrium ceases to exist as a stable attractor. Two empirical sources support the model. A 46-year longitudinal index for Spain, constructed from 62 verified organisms in the Official State Gazette, yields R2=0.515 in the central mechanistic test, with five of six tests significant at p<0.001. A panel of all 27 EU democracies using Digital Society Project v7 data confirms monotonic growth in the asymmetry index across the full 2000-2022 period.

title: Legal Empowerment under Autocracy: A Field Experiment in Rural China

detail.title: Legal Empowerment under Autocracy: A Field Experiment in Rural China
detail.abstract: Autocrats expanding legal access face a dilemma: channeling grievances into official institutions can stabilize rule, but it can also empower citizens to press claims. I evaluate this tradeoff with a 20-week cluster-randomized experiment across 70 Chinese villages embedded in a government village-lawyer program. Treatments randomized the messenger (village chief versus lawyer) and incentives (material benefits, with or without public social recognition). Chief-led mobilization boosts lecture attendance and modestly raises local political trust, but it does not match lawyer-led mobilization in sustained legal service use or conflict reduction. Lawyer-led mobilization instead increases legal knowledge, consultations, and rights-claiming while lowering political trust. Public social recognition reduces attrition, converts attendance into consultations, and strengthens longer-run civic engagement, especially among politically connected residents. Authoritarian legality therefore hinges on intermediaries and incentives: political brokers secure incorporation without substantive empowerment, whereas professionals cultivate deeper empowerment at the expense of regime legitimacy.

detail.abstract: Sexual harassment awareness training is a key tool to combat sexual harassment, which affects nearly 205 million people in the workplace (ILO, 2022). This paper provides the first randomized evaluation of such training in collaboration with colleges in Delhi, India, to study its impact on sexual harassment. I randomly assigned men to receive this training, with empathy-building, and collected reports of sexual harassment from women in their classes. The training significantly reduced sexual harassment for upto 3 years and altered men's perceptions of social disapproval more than their intrinsic attitudes. It also led to a long-lasting reduction in classroom romantic relationships. A mechanism experiment suggests this is due to women finding it difficult to judge men's quality when social disapproval generates a pooling equilibrium. A similar intervention for women had no detectable effects. Finally, men's training increased women's labor market engagement without affecting their mental well-being or test scores.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a broad discussion of efforts to reform Medicaid not simply in size but also in its very construction, with a focus on maximizing the efficiency of this program. We begin with a high-level overview of the current structure of America’s healthcare safety net for the poor and disabled, including Medicaid, noting that the piecemeal nature of Medicaid’s evolution has created a complex program bringing together various populations, providers, operating models, and revenue streams. We then briefly examine implications of recently proposed reforms to this system, which largely hold the structure of the program fixed and focus on marginal changes to financing and eligibility. In the final part of the paper, we propose a broader and more fundamental set of reforms that acknowledge that Medicaid’s contemporary size and scope require a different structure than those of its smaller historical predecessors. We propose policies that foster lower-cost-structure business models for safety-net healthcare providers in order to expand the number of these providers and more aggressively steer Medicaid patients to them. The goal is to use Medicaid’s existing funding to provide easy access to basic healthcare services provided by a more abundant supply of safety-net healthcare facilities that work exclusively (or almost exclusively) with patients from this program.

title: Welcome to the Trump Administration’s Board of Immigration Appeals. The Immigrant Always Loses
affiliations: University of Georgia School of Law

detail.title: Welcome to the Trump Administration’s Board of Immigration Appeals. The Immigrant Always Loses
detail.abstract: Volume 29 of the Board of Immigration Appeals’ precedential decisions is not a collection of independent legal judgments. It is a project. The Trump administration has used the Attorney General’s self-referral power and a reconstituted, ideologically aligned Board to issue approximately 89 precedential decisions, at more than three times the historical pace, in its first fourteen months. The goal is to engineer a body of precedents that reliably produces one result: removal. This Article organizes this body of decisions into four primary categories: (1) narrowing relief for noncitizens alleging persecution; (2) accelerating the removal of vulnerable persons—including crime victims and abused children—who are on congressionally authorized pathways to status; (3) expanding mandatory detention while narrowing discretionary release; and (4) maximizing the immigration consequences of criminal history. An emerging fifth category reveals a Board that weaponizes its own procedural delays against the litigants whose claims it has sat on for years. A parallel set of rule changes—most recently an interim final rule that a federal court partially vacated in early March—has sought to insulate most deportation orders from any meaningful appellate review. The Article identifies three implications of this project for federal courts. First, Loper Bright’s elimination of Chevron deference, combined with the Board's institutional redesign and the uniformity of its outcomes, undermines any claim to persuasive weight, and many of the Board’s decisions should not survive de novo statutory review. Second, the exhaustion doctrine’s justifications collapse when the administrative body to be exhausted has been rebuilt to foreordain a result. Third, the Board’s selective deployment of the civil/criminal distinction, invoking it to deny protections when it benefits the government, and to exclude favorable criminal law developments when it benefits the noncitizen, is itself a doctrinal choice that post-Loper Bright courts should examine without deference, as it has invariably cut against the noncitizen.

detail.abstract: We introduce Reflexivity Kernel Spectroscopy (RKS), a system-identification framework that continuously estimates the market's multiscale, multi-asset flow-to-price transfer operator-the reflexivity kernel-and uses its spectral invariants to decompose realized covariance into an endogenous, flow-driven component and an exogenous innovation residual. The operator is estimated subject to three hard admissibility constraints: cumulative positive semi-definiteness, cross-impact reciprocity, and no-positive-expected-profit round-trip proxies, enforced as unittestable optimization gates rather than post-hoc checks. Constraint violations produce first-class failure artifacts rather than silent fallback. On a calibrated BTC/ETH synthetic baseline (lags = 4, CLARABEL interior-point solver, cumulative nuclear-norm regularization), the exact constrained estimator achieves 100% primary admissible window survival, 0% PSD failure, mean reflexivity share of 75-82%, and out-of-sample R-squared of 76-83%. A free empirical study using Binance Vision trade archives confirms correct pipeline execution on real public data and produces a coherent calm-versus-stress operator contrast, though depth-based falsification requires full orderbook replay and remains the stated next step. We demarcate explicitly what the current evidence establishes, what it does not, and what data closes the remaining observability gap. The central claim-that the reflexivity kernel and its spectrum constitute a new market-state primitive upstream of returns, correlations, and factor exposures-is supported by the calibration and structural admissibility evidence but requires stress-event validation on thesis-grade L2 depth data before it can be treated as an empirically complete result.

detail.abstract: The Do The Right Math initiative proposes that many organizational and financial decisions suffer from a structural weakness: assumptions are often formed implicitly and conclusions are reached without ensuring that actions logically follow from explicitly defined premises. Drawing on the formal structure of game theory-players, strategies, and payoff ranges-the framework positions disciplined decision-making as a safeguard against both cognitive bias and uncritical delegation to artificial intelligence systems. This paper extends that philosophy into a real-field operational setting: U.S. equity portfolio management through the www.pcdomoney.com application. The applied system is structured as a human-in-the-loop, event-driven investment process incorporating a strategic-actor lens, where politically or economically influential actors like Donald Trump may generate informational shocks that trigger portfolio reassessment. The empirical objective is to document the evolution of the "DoTheRightMath Fund" portfolio methodology from 17 June 2025 through 13 March 2026 and to compare its performance against three baselines: (i) a broad market benchmark (S&P 500), (ii) a cohort-based 11-stock portfolio constructed through an LLM-only token-driven selection workflow, and (iii) a fully systematic AI-managed ETF benchmark, the Amplify AI Powered Equity ETF (AIEQ). Across five completed cohorts, the DTRM Fund produced a compounded return of 32.99%, versus 9.17% for the ChatGPT Fund, 8.75% for the S&P 500, and 5.98% for the aligned AIEQ peer. The results suggest that investment outcomes depend not only on predictive model quality, but also on the architecture by which information is translated into action. The central contribution of the paper is therefore not a new automated trading algorithm, but the empirical formalization of structured decision-making under uncertainty, where artificial intelligence functions as strategic augmentation while final portfolio actions remain governed by accountable human intervention.

detail.abstract: We introduce Constraint Shadow-Price Tomography (CSPT), a market metrology system that reconstructs the latent dual state of financial intermediation constraints by inverting a sensor array of persistent law-of-one-price wedges across spot, derivative, and funding markets. The central primitive is the Market Dual State-a time-versioned, non-negative vector Lambda_t whose components are the implied shadow prices of binding intermediation constraints, recovered via a deterministic convex inverse solve subject to non-negativity, temporal smoothing, and explicit identifiability diagnostics. Applied to the March 2020 Treasury market stress episode using public CIP, Treasury cash-futures basis, and swap spread data, the system recovers a three-coordinate constraint state that peaks at Lambda_{balance-sheet} = 152.91 on March 27-the date of the Federal Reserve's emergency repo facility expansion-with a single-day move of +19.11. Quarterend identification following the difference-indifferences design of Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018) yields p = 0.000777, confirming that the balance-sheet coordinate responds to known regulatory reporting windows. A targeted jackknife diagnostic shows that the balance-sheet and secured-funding coordinates are genuinely separated: dropping balance-sheet-dominant sensors shifts the secured-funding coordinate by only 2.6% in the three-family build, versus 8.3% in the two-family baseline. The out-of-family prediction test-estimating Lambda_t from CIP and Treasury basis only, then pricing withheld swap spread observations-yields a mean MAE of 18.68 bp and a latest-date MAE of 3.10 bp, establishing cross-market constraint coherence. The system is designed to emit failure artifacts rather than smooth over poor identification: when the loading matrix is ill-conditioned, CSPT reports 'cannot separate' rather than producing spurious precision. The central claim-that law-of-one-price deviations are tomographic projections of a latent constraint dual state rather than separate anomalies-is supported by the empirical evidence reported here and constitutes a new measurement primitive upstream of returns, factors, and conventional liquidity proxies.

detail.abstract:
Evaluating the health impacts of climate action is increasingly important as governments and international organisations expand mitigation and adaptation efforts. Beyond environmental outcomes, these policies can generate substantial health co-benefits, yet these are often insufficiently captured in the economic evaluation frameworks used to inform policy decisions. A recent scoping review conducted by the authors identified significant heterogeneity in the methods used to assess the health co-benefits of climate action, including cost–benefit, cost-effectiveness, and cost-utility analyses, macroeconomic modelling, and toolkit-based approaches. While this methodological diversity reflects the interdisciplinary nature of climate–health research, it presents challenges for comparability, transparency, and policy relevance.
This paper examines five key methodological areas that shape how the health impacts of climate action are valued and interpreted in economic evaluations: the Social Cost of Carbon, the Value of a Statistical Life, equity considerations, macroeconomic modelling approaches, and discounting practices. Building on the findings of the initial scoping review, targeted in-depth reviews were conducted for each topic using the literature already gathered. The paper synthesises these findings to assess current practices, identify methodological challenges, and highlight areas where greater clarity and consistency are needed. Overall, the study aims to contribute to ongoing methodological and policy debates on how economic evaluation can more effectively capture the efficiency, distributional impacts, and long-term sustainability of climate–health interventions.

detail.abstract: This paper, Tesla's Road in India: Disruptive Innovation or Innovative Disruption in Trade Policy?, critically examines Tesla's entry into the Indian market, with a particular focus on the intersection of disruptive innovation and trade policy. Drawing on economic theory and policy analysis, the study explores whether Tesla's approach to market penetration and technological advancement constitutes a disruptive innovation within the automotive sector, or represents an innovative disruption in the wider trade policy arena. By analysing Tesla's strategies in the context of India’s regulatory framework, market structure, and evolving global trade dynamics, this paper identifies key tensions between technological breakthroughs and policy structures. Furthermore, it investigates how these innovations challenge traditional trade barriers, such as tariffs and non-tariff measures, and the implications for both domestic and international stakeholders. Ultimately, the paper provides a nuanced understanding of how Tesla's market entry exemplifies shifting paradigms in trade policy and the broader implications for global trade governance in an era increasingly shaped by technological advances.

detail.abstract: Political party funding in India between 1964 and 1990 developed within a political economy where governments controlled access to key economic permissions such as industrial licensing, imports, foreign exchange, procurement, and land. In such a regime, political access carried high economic value, and political competition generated continuous demand for money to sustain organisation, candidates, and campaigns. This paper explains party revenue not as a single stream of "donations," but as a layered system combining central party funds, state unit funds, candidate-level spending, and broker-mediated circuits. It compares party funding models by ideology and organisation, highlighting the Communist movement's cadre-based revenue logic and the Swatantra Party's role in legitimising openly pro-business funding orientations. It treats the 1969 corporate donation ban and mid-1980s relaxation as turning points, while emphasising that political money repeatedly shifted form rather than disappearing when rules changed.

detail.abstract: How do authoritarian regimes make law accessible without letting it become politically dangerous? I argue that when states delegate legal aid to frontline lawyers, they separate legal recognition from legal empowerment: citizens may receive courteous, legally framed acknowledgment without the actionable guidance needed to press claims. I test this argument with a nationwide audit experiment of China's state-run legal-aid hotline system based on 3,200 randomized calls across 302 cities. Politically sensitive and socially disadvantaged callers still receive answers, but those answers are less claim-enabling: minority-name and petition cues reduce substantive guidance and concrete referrals, while symbolic accommodation remains available. Positive evaluation raises both substantive and symbolic responsiveness, whereas complaint pressure improves visible service more than claim-enabling assistance. These findings show how authoritarian regimes can widen access to law while withholding the forms of assistance most likely to generate empowerment.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of climate change-induced risk on bank profitability in the G7 countries from 2001 to 2022. Using dynamic panel GMM estimation to analyse banking industry data with climate risk factors, we find that climate risk has a negative effect on bank profitability. The study also demonstrates that bank liquidity creation plays a key role in transmitting the adverse impact of climate risk on bank profitability. Additionally, the results of the study are robust and withstand different measures of bank liquidity creation. Furthermore, our empirical findings indicate that the influence of climate risk factors is consistent, even for banks primarily focussed on the insurance business. These findings suggest that policymakers may need to implement climate risk management policies to mitigate the detrimental effects of climate change on the banking sector.

detail.abstract: This paper is a critical and analytical response to the question “The critical question for developing countries is not whether the state intervenes in the economy but how it intervenes”, and examines the political economy of development by addressing the central question for developing countries: not whether the state should intervene in the economy, but how it should intervene. Through a comprehensive analysis of various models of state involvement, the paper explores the nuanced ways in which different forms of intervention shape economic outcomes in the Global South. It delves into the historical and contemporary debates surrounding state-led development, analysing the role of government policies in fostering industrialisation, addressing inequality, and promoting sustainable growth. The paper assesses the challenges and opportunities faced by developing nations in designing effective interventions that balance market forces with state oversight, particularly in light of globalisation and external pressures. Drawing on case studies from diverse regions, the study highlights the importance of context-specific policies and the need for a flexible, strategic approach to state intervention that takes into account both domestic realities and international dynamics. By critically engaging with the political economy of development, this paper offers insights into how state intervention can be a tool for inclusive and transformative economic change in developing countries.

detail.abstract: This study proposes a comprehensive modeling framework for mortgage prepayment risk, a critical factor in the valuation of fixed-income portfolios and Net Interest Margin (NIM) optimization. Integrating classification-based machine learning and survival analysis, we analyze a dataset of 148,938 mortgage records from Freddie Mac. We evaluate Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting (GBM) alongside a Cox Proportional Hazards model. Experimental results indicate that Gradient Boosting achieves superior predictive performance with an AUC-ROC of 0.776 and an F1score of 0.679, while the Cox model provides temporal interpretability with a C-index of 0.676. SHAP analysis identifies interest rate spreads, loan age, and credit scores as the primary drivers of prepayment behavior, offering actionable insights for proactive capital management.

detail.title: Trade Secret Law's On-Sale Bar

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rutgers Law School Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Rutgers Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The on-sale bar is a well-established rule in patent law. Once an invention has been placed “on sale” for over a year, it cannot thereafter be patented. Trade secret law, at first glance, is different. Trade secret law can indefinitely protect information relating to a product, even after it has been marketed. Consider the famous example of the Coca-Cola formula. The formula is still claimed as a trade secret, even though the soft drink has been sold to the public for over a century. If employees were to leave Coca-Cola with the formula and use it to develop a competing soft drink, Coca-Cola would still have a claim under trade secret law. However, this article shows that trade secret law contains a legal analog to patent law’s on-sale bar. This is the requirement that a trade secret not be “readily ascertainable through proper means.” The effect of trade secret law’s readily-ascertainable doctrine is surprisingly similar to patent law’s on-sale bar: If trade secrets can “readily” be ascertained through reverse engineering products on the market, then trade secrecy protection is unavailable.

This similarity is not a coincidence. The drafters of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (UTSA)—which provides the basis for the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA)—adopted the “not-readily-ascertainable” limitation from a line of common law cases because they worried companies would indefinitely rely on trade secrecy after marketing products to the public, and that this would impoverish the “public domain” and interfere with patent law’s policy goals. Thus, they added a provision to the UTSA clarifying that trade secret rights end once reverse engineering becomes “readily” achievable—even if the defendant herself did not get the information that way. Despite its statutory basis, courts misunderstand and misapply the readily-ascertainable doctrine. Some courts misconstrue it entirely. Others wrongly place the burden on the defendant to prove information is readily ascertainable, rather than the reverse. Still other courts understand the rule in theory, but shy away from holding information is readily ascertainable, even in the face of overwhelming evidence of easy reverse engineering. The result is that some information is likely being over-protected. 

As a solution, the article proposes a type of on-sale bar for trade secret law. Trade secret law’s on-sale bar should be viewed as a species of the statutory requirement that a trade secret not be readily ascertainable through proper means. The defendant’s initial burden is (only) to show that an “on-sale” event has occurred—meaning, in this context, that the trade secret holder or a third party had already marketed products embedding the secrets at the time of the alleged misappropriation. Once the defendant shows this, the burden is on the plaintiff to prove reverse engineering would be time-consuming, expensive, or otherwise difficult. The plaintiff must provide specific evidence, including an estimated timeframe for how long reverse engineering the secret would take. If the plaintiff fails to do this on summary judgment, and certainly by the time of trial, the court should hold for the defendant as a matter of law.

detail.abstract: Central bank communication on financial stability has been less studied than on monetary policy. Our paper aims to contribute to the growing literature in this area. Our focus is the region of Central Europe, where financial sectors are intertwined through close cross-border ownership, and about half of the countries are members of the euro area. Using large language models (LLMs) combined with country-specific contextual analysis, we study executive summaries of Financial Stability Reports (FSRs) published since the early 2000s by seven Central, Eastern, and Southeastern European (CESEE) central banks, as well as by Austria and the European Central Bank (ECB). We construct a novel financial stability sentiment index and document that central bank communication is strongly risk-focused, most notably in the case of the ECB. In addition, prior to the Global Financial Crisis, the Austrian central bank was much less concerned than other central banks in the region although Austria plays a pivotal role in the financial system in the region. Our analysis of the link between financial stability sentiment communication and macroprudential policy action highlights that many central banks actively use and communicate about borrower-based measures, while most countries activated non-zero counter-cyclical capital buffers belatedly or not at all. Finally, comparing central banks’ communication on financial stability and monetary policy, we find that euro area national central banks and the ECB’s FSR communicated about the rising risks of post-Covid inflation in a timely manner, ahead of the ECB’s monetary policy communication.

detail.abstract: The United States’ innovation edge rests on its ability to draw on the best talent from around the world. Yet, the laws that govern high-skilled immigration have barely moved since 1990 for permanent residency and since 2000 for temporary work visas, leaving them misaligned with the size and needs of today’s economy. Employers register for more than three times as many H-1Bs as are available each year, which are then awarded at random rather than on the basis of merit. For permanent residency, just 140,000 employment-based green cards are issued annually, most of which go to spouses and children rather than to workers themselves. The resulting backlogs now exceed one million, leaving many workers stuck in less productive jobs and discouraging future talent from coming to the US altogether. This paper charts the alphabet soup of high-skilled immigration pathways—F-1/OPT, J-1, H-1B, O-1A, EB-1, EB-2, and EB-3—demonstrating how inflexible and outdated rules have undermined the scale, selectivity, and retention of global talent. It proposes reforms to make immigration a renewed national strength: expanding green cards, piloting a pointsbased system for permanent residency, and launching a government talent-scouting arm. Together, these steps would realign US immigration policy with national ambition and restore its role in fueling American innovation and economic leadership.

detail.abstract: Despite strong economic conditions, survey data reveal substantial economic worry and discontent among Americans. Pew survey data from 2024 indicated that “strengthening the economy” was Americans’ top policy priority, above “defending against terrorism,” “reducing crime,” and “dealing with immigration” (Pew 2024). A separate Pew survey from that same year found that only 53 percent of Americans believe that the “American Dream,” defined as the idea that anyone can achieve success in the United States through hard work and determination, is still possible (Borelli 2024). Advancing broad economic prosperity requires an understanding of the economic well-being of American households, as well as potential contributors to widespread economic malaise. With that goal, this piece highlights current evidence on household financial well-being through six facts and accompanying figures. First, we document trends in earnings and income growth across the wage distribution as well as by educational attainment, gender, and geography. Second, we highlight trends in the costs of two salient household budget items: housing and healthcare.

detail.abstract: This Article sheds light on the rise of BlackRock and Vanguard as major institutional investors in Brazil. Over recent decades, the American “Big Two” asset managers have become the world’s largest, extending their reach into international markets. Yet their presence outside the United States remains underexplored, limiting a deeper understanding of their economic influence and their role in driving global trends toward ownership concentration and common ownership. This Article helps fill that gap by tracing their expansion into Brazil’s public equity market. Drawing on S&P Capital IQ data, it shows that BlackRock and Vanguard increased their combined share of the market capitalization of 191 B3-listed companies by 7.6 percentage points between 2008 and 2023, reaching 9.6%. Their investments were especially pronounced in the materials, IT, and energy sectors. By 2023, the Big Two held ownership stakes of 5% or more in nearly half of the sample, and in seven companies BlackRock alone held more than 10%, emerging as the largest shareholder in two. In doing so, this study provides the first systematic account of the Big Two’s footprint in Brazil and highlights key policy concerns for further investigation regarding their rise in markets dominated by controlling shareholders.

detail.title: Default Risk and Liquidity Provision of Sovereign Debt
detail.abstract: Sovereign bonds are widely used as collateral to support credit transactions, and the haircuts—discounts on asset values when pledged as collateral—are closely linked to sovereign default risk. We extend a standard model of sovereign default by incorporating the liquidity role of sovereign bonds as collateral and study the implications of this liquidity channel for default risk and interest rates. Taking the government's default decision as given, we show that a rise in default probability increases the haircut on sovereign bonds, reducing their liquidity premium. However, this effect is mitigated by a general equilibrium effect whereby a reduction in the effective stock of collateral raises liquidity premia for both risk-free assets and risky sovereign bonds. We also endogenize the government's default decision and show that the liquidity role of sovereign bonds reduces the government’s incentive to default by generating an endogenous cost of default.

detail.abstract: We quantify the effect of severe weather shocks on the US economy in an environment in which the economy can switch between periods of financial stability and financial instability, like the Great Recession. We estimate a New Keynesian dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model with banks and severe weather events. We show that severe weather shocks: 1) have a negative impact on real and financial US variables, sizable only in periods of financial instability, but muted effects on nominal variables; 2) are never a relevant source of business cycles fluctuations; 3) transmit mainly via a deterioration in the quality of capital.
