detail.abstract:
Financial education is widely promoted as a key strategy for improving personal financial decision-making. Despite these efforts, many individuals continue to experience persistent financial challenges, including limited savings buffers, reliance on unsecured debt, and ongoing financial stress. These outcomes suggest that financial knowledge alone may not fully explain differences in financial wellbeing. This paper examines the behavioural constraints that can limit the translation of financial knowledge into consistent financial action.

Drawing on insights from behavioural finance and evidence from the Financial Conduct Authority’s Financial Lives Survey 2024, the study explores how behavioural and contextual factors interact with financial knowledge to influence financial outcomes. Particular attention is given to the roles of financial stress, impulsive decision-making, accountability structures, and the consistency of financial habits.

The paper introduces the concept of behavioural stability as a framework for understanding financial behaviour over time. Behavioural stability refers to an individual’s ability to maintain financially beneficial behaviours, such as disciplined spending and regular saving, despite the presence of stress, temptation, or changing financial circumstances. Using descriptive patterns from survey data, the analysis illustrates how indicators associated with financial pressure and behavioural regulation appear more closely related to financial wellbeing than measures of financial knowledge alone.

The findings suggest that while financial literacy remains an important component of financial capability, it is not sufficient on its own to explain variations in financial resilience. Behavioural and contextual influences play a central role in shaping financial outcomes. Recognising these influences may help inform more effective approaches to financial education, financial product design, and policies aimed at improving long-term financial stability.

title: Can Models with Idiosyncratic Risk Solve the Equity Premium Puzzle? Redux *
affiliations: University of California, Davis, University of California, Davis and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco

detail.title: Can Models with Idiosyncratic Risk Solve the Equity Premium Puzzle? Redux *
detail.abstract: Can idiosyncratic risk explain the equity premium? We revisit this question using a novel measure of imperfect risk sharing, implied by a large class of heterogeneous-agent models, constructed using household-level panel data. We identify a group of households-with relatively high income but low net-worth-whose consumption is sufficiently volatile and risky to explain 94% of the observed U.S. Sharpe ratio. In contrast, the consumption dynamics of high net-worth individuals predict a negative Sharpe ratio and so do not constitute the relevant pricing factor, consistent with models featuring wealth motives.

title: The Evolving Collaborative Investment Model: Innovation in Government-Institutional Investor Partnerships
affiliations: , Independent Consultant, Stanford University and Stanford University

detail.title: The Evolving Collaborative Investment Model: Innovation in Government-Institutional Investor Partnerships
detail.abstract: The collaborative investment model ("Collaborative model") is premised on the formation of innovative, aligned structures to facilitate the flow of institutional investor capital into long-term assets that urgently require investment, such as infrastructure, renewable energy, and economic development. While investment structuring among institutional investors is a key component of the Collaborative model, governments also play an important role by providing the right frameworks to attract long-term capital. In certain countries, the role of governments and institutional investors is evolving into a new form of partnership, whereby institutional investors can invest directly with and through government-controlled entities. This paper highlights the salient features of this evolution of the Collaborative model, from the perspectives of both host governments and committed institutional investors. Some of these features, although originally contemplated by the Collaborative model, challenge conventional assumptions about what is required for successful interactions between government and institutional investors. The paper also examines the conditions under which these government-controlled entities can be successfully replicated in other countries.

title: Enduring Impact: A Manifesto for Institutional Durability
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Enduring Impact: A Manifesto for Institutional Durability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: Organizations dedicated to social and environmental impact must be intentionally designed for endurance, not merely for short-term influence or growth. Many nonprofit and mission-driven enterprises were built under assumptions of political, financial, and regulatory stability that no longer hold, leaving them vulnerable to disruption when funding contracts, policies shift, or leadership transitions occur. The article contends that meaningful impact requires institutional durability created through governance structures, financial systems, leadership succession and organizational culture deliberately engineered to withstand volatility while preserving mission fidelity. By treating endurance as a core design objective from inception, these enduring impact organizations can maintain their capacity to serve stakeholders and pursue long-term social progress despite inevitable cycles of instability. This article calls for a shift across the impact sector from a focus on rapid expansion and innovation toward structural resilience, stewardship, and generational continuity.

title: AI Masquerade: Hiding Employee Expansion in the AI Era

detail.title: AI Masquerade: Hiding Employee Expansion in the AI Era
detail.abstract: This paper documents a fundamental regime shift in how the equity market values corporate labor expansion following the release of ChatGPT. Prior to ChatGPT, job creation and stock market valuations moved closely together, but this relationship decouples sharply afterward. Using earnings call transcripts, I show that the stock market previously rewarded hiring signals but penalizes them in the post-ChatGPT period. This is because investors interpret labor expansion as evidence that firms are behind on adopting AI. The penalty is mitigated when firms simultaneously signal that they are adopting AI to substitute for workers. In response, firms that are actively hiring either curtail their hiring disclosures or, when they do disclose, simultaneously signal AI adoption as a substitute for workers---a pattern I term the AI Masquerade. Yet firms that still disclose hiring intentions are systematically underpriced in the short run, despite being more productive than firms without any hiring signals. This generates predictable long-run excess returns as the market corrects its initial over-penalization. An analogous portfolio strategy based on job postings generates no such returns over the same period, implying that the mispricing is not driven by a risk premium associated with labor demand itself.

title: Real Time Risk Dynamics in the Financial Sector
affiliations: , University of Florence - Department of Economics and Management and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Real Time Risk Dynamics in the Financial Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The views expressed herein are those of the authors and should not be attributed to the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Reserve System.

detail.abstract: Building on the structural model of default proposed by Nagel and Purnanandam (2020) [Banks' Risk Dynamics and Distance to Default. Review of Financial Studies, 2020, 33, 2421-2467], we develop a semi-analytical, market-based framework to estimate default risk for a wide range of financial institutions-including banks, insurance companies, and broker-dealers-whose business models involve leverage and maturity transformation. Our approach accounts for the compound option nature of financial firms' equity and the staggered maturity of asset portfolios, enabling the construction of a novel, multi-dimensional distance-to-default measure. Using observable equity and CDS market prices, we estimate key structural parameters-including asset volatility, systematic exposure, and market leverage-at daily frequency via a nonlinear state-space model. Institutionlevel distance-to-defaults are aggregated to produce a Financial Systemic Risk indicator, which captures correlations across asset cohorts, aligns with established systemic risk measures, and successfully tracks episodes of elevated financial stress, including the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank crisis.

title: Why AI Adoption Fails: A Constraint-Based Diagnostic Model for Organizational Readiness

detail.title: Why AI Adoption Fails: A Constraint-Based Diagnostic Model for Organizational Readiness

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence use has broadened quickly, but sustained organizational adoption remains uneven. McKinsey's 2025 global survey reports that 88 percent of respondents say their organizations use AI in at least one business function, yet nearly two-thirds remain in experimentation or piloting and only 39 percent report any enterprise-level EBIT impact from AI use (McKinsey & Company, 2025). Gartner projected that at least 30 percent of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025 (Gartner, 2024), while RAND notes estimates that more than 80 percent of AI projects fail (Ryseff et al., 2024). These patterns suggest that technical capability and organizational adoption are not the same problem. This paper proposes that many stalled AI initiatives are best understood as a constraint-diagnosis problem. Existing readiness, change-management, and adoption frameworks often describe broad conditions associated with implementation success, but they are less effective at identifying which single human or organizational factor is most limiting progress in a given system at a given moment. As a result, organizations frequently improve visible symptoms while the binding constraint remains untouched. To address that gap, this paper introduces THE WHEEL Framework™, a conceptual diagnostic architecture for organizational readiness. The framework integrates five established research traditions-theory of constraints, psychological safety, social identity, innovation diffusion, and trust in automation-and organizes readiness across eight dimensions: Identity, Psychological Safety, Workflow Integration, AI Environment, Social Dynamics, Leadership Signals, Learning Depth, and Measurement. Its central claim is that readiness is often asymmetric: one weak dimension can disproportionately limit adoption and distort the symptoms observed elsewhere. The paper contributes a constraint-based perspective to the AI adoption literature. It positions adoption failure not simply as a technology, training, or change-management problem, but as a socio-technical bottleneck problem shaped by identity, trust, workflow design, leadership behavior, learning systems, and feedback loops. The assessment instrument, item set, weighting logic, and scoring implementation are intentionally omitted. This publication is limited to the conceptual architecture and research argument.

title: Agent Selection and Belief Polarization in Distributive Bargaining
affiliations: and Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth

detail.title: Agent Selection and Belief Polarization in Distributive Bargaining
detail.abstract: Many negotiations-from legal disputes to labor contracts-are conducted through agents rather than directly by principals. While significant attention has been given to the misalignment of interests between principals and agents, little is known about how the process of selecting an agent affects bargaining outcomes. Across four preregistered experiments (N = 4,385), we show that principals systematically choose agents who go on to make overly aggressive offers. Principals on each side preferentially select agents whose beliefs about fair and achievable outcomes are especially favorable to their respective side. Thus, they send pairs of agents to the bargaining table whose expectations are strongly opposed and who are therefore more likely to reach impasse. Agent selection leads to worse outcomes than if principals chose randomly or negotiated on their own behalf, and outcomes could be improved by unilaterally selecting less aggressive agents. We document these patterns across distinct bargaining environments: an ultimatum-style settlement task and a real-time, open-ended negotiation.

title: Beyond the Blind Pool: How Private Asset-backed Structured Products Reshape Risk and Return
affiliations: , , Harvard Business School - Finance Unit, Bella Private Markets and

detail.title: Beyond the Blind Pool: How Private Asset-backed Structured Products Reshape Risk and Return
detail.abstract: Private markets have become a significant component of investor portfolios, offering the potential for enhanced risk-adjusted returns relative to public assets. However, structural features like illiquidity, irregular cash flows, information asymmetries, performance dispersion, and constrained access to private markets complicate portfolio construction and risk management practices. This paper examines the rise of private asset-linked structured products, particularly collateralized fund obligations (CFOs), as a mechanism for transforming portfolios of private assets into securities with distinct risk-return profiles. We analyze how these structures approach diversification, utilize tranching, alter cash flow timing, and address regulatory capital considerations; while also highlighting important limitations to these products. Drawing on academic literature, industry evidence, and quantitative analysis, we evaluate the role of CFOs within a broader portfolio context, showcasing potential benefits and structural complexities. The paper contributes a consolidated framework for assessing the investment implications of this emerging segment of structured finance.

title: Dynamic Landscape of Monetary Policy Communication in India

detail.title: Dynamic Landscape of Monetary Policy Communication in India
detail.abstract: Communication has evolved as an effective monetary policy tool for reducing surprise elements and anchoring expectations of economic agents. This article explores the dynamic landscape of monetary policy communication in India, encompassing two recent crisis events, viz., the Covid-19 pandemic and geopolitical conflict in Ukraine. The relative emphasis on specific topics in monetary policy meetings varied in response to changing economic conditions. The tone of communication on inflation, derived using a customised dictionary, is found to be significant in shaping the market expectations. This impact is particularly evident for medium-term overnight indexed swap (OIS) rates. The influence of communication is also observed to be higher during tightening phase.

title: Remote Sensing Applications for Policy: An Assessment of Agricultural Commodity Arrivals

detail.title: Remote Sensing Applications for Policy: An Assessment of Agricultural Commodity Arrivals
detail.abstract: Timely and reliable information on crop production is a key element for gauging future inflationary trends. The study explores the utility of remote sensing data for policy analysis with a focus on pulses. Using satellite imagery-based Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), vegetation growth is derived by suitable seasonal filtering and temporal aggregation. The results suggest that vegetation growth has significant ability to provide reasonably good assessment of commodity arrivals in mandis, well in advance. Further, geospatial modelling using location coordinates indicates the presence of spatial heterogeneity.

title: From Pixels To Plots: Synthesizing Remote Sensing Into Crop Production Estimation

detail.title: From Pixels To Plots: Synthesizing Remote Sensing Into Crop Production Estimation
detail.abstract: In the overarching realm of national accounts, the precision of crop production data is crucial, considering its inter-dynamics with macroeconomic factors. Timely evaluation of the supply-side situation can provide early signals for undertaking proactive policy measures. Publication lags and subsequent revisions in official statistics on foodgrain production pose limitations for their operational utility. Complexities of agricultural ecosystems and evolving climatic conditions underscore the need for a sophisticated approach. The paper makes an attempt to design a generic framework for synthesizing remote sensing data for in-season monitoring of crop conditions and production nowcasting, aiming at enhancing accuracy and timeliness. The framework is designed to be customizable and scalable, and a bottom-up aggregation approach is followed for arriving at country-level estimates, considering the geo-spatial variation in data. Vegetation, soil moisture conditions, and temperature effects are analyzed along with area coverage. An empirical application carried out for pulses demonstrates the value gain of incorporating such new-age data and provides encouragement for further refinements for the operational use of remote sensing, weather, and climatic data for data-driven policy making.

title: Geopolitical Risk and Equity Returns: Evidence From Global Markets
affiliations: EMLYON Business School and Lumière University Lyon 2

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk and Equity Returns: Evidence From Global Markets
detail.abstract: Geopolitical events have emerged as critical drivers of financial market uncertainty. We show that their impacts have heterogeneous consequences around the globe, both at the aggregate index level and for individual stocks. Using countryspecific geopolitical risk measures, this paper examines the persistent effects of geopolitical risk on global equity markets and firm-level returns. At the market level, we document an immediate and negative response of equity returns to increases in geopolitical risk, with stronger effects observed in emerging markets. At the stock level, controlling for standard asset pricing factors, we uncover substantial heterogeneity in firms' exposure, both in magnitude and timing. Firms in developed markets tend to respond contemporaneously, whereas those in emerging markets exhibit delayed reactions. We further explore the investment implications by forming portfolios based on firm-level geopolitical risk exposure. Evidence from the U.S. and Chinese equity markets shows that portfolios constructed using contemporaneous exposure information outperform market benchmarks likely due to look-ahead bias. However, those based on lagged estimates largely track benchmark performance. Overall, our findings highlight geopolitical risk as a persistent pricing factor with meaningful implications for asset pricing and portfolio management beyond extreme events.

title: Technology Investment Governance Under Deep Uncertainty: The Case for Annual Portfolio Models in Public Infrastructure
affiliations: University of Liverpool,  and

detail.title: Technology Investment Governance Under Deep Uncertainty: The Case for Annual Portfolio Models in Public Infrastructure
detail.abstract:
Technology investment forecasting has repeatedly proved unreliable for large-scale public infrastructure. Canonical tools — net present value appraisal and discounted cash flow modelling — require stable probability distributions for demand, costs, and discount rates that empirical evidence shows cannot be reliably estimated over decade-long or longer timescales of major infrastructure commitments. A 2026 European Court of Auditors report confirms that major EU transport flagship megaprojects have experienced average delays of 17 years across 5 monitored projects, with real cost increases of 47% across 8 flagship programmes assessed in the previous audit cycle; the European LNG infrastructure build-out locked in capacity just as European energy demand forecasts began to diverge. This paper argues that the problem is not forecasting quality but forecasting architecture: governments treat technology investment forecasts as commitment devices rather than decision inputs, producing governance structures that cannot adapt when forecasts fail.

Drawing on three bodies of literature — Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty (DMDU), ecological rationality and fast-and-frugal heuristics, and CAPEX-bias regulatory economics — we develop the Annual Portfolio Model as a technology governance framework. The model replaces project-by-project capital commitments with annually revised expenditure envelopes, staged commitments with explicit exit options, and simple fast-and-frugal prioritisation rules that remain robust to forecast error. We illustrate the framework through four cases: Channel Tunnel governance failure, sunk-cost exit decisions, EU LNG and TEN-T infrastructure, and UK digital government portfolio reform. Implications for technology governance research and public policy practice are developed.

title: Tokenization as a Supply Shock: A Nonlinear and Asymmetric Framework for AI Economics (V2)

detail.title: Tokenization as a Supply Shock: A Nonlinear and Asymmetric Framework for AI Economics (V2)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a conceptual framework to interpret the economic impact of artificial intelligence (AI) through the lens of “tokenization.” We define tokenization as the transformation of cognitive outputs and production processes into standardized, replicable digital units (“tokens”) with near-zero marginal cost.

We argue that the AI revolution constitutes a large-scale supply shock concentrated in tokenizable sectors, leading to asymmetric effects across the economy. While token production expands and prices decline, overall welfare may increase due to expanded exchange and accessibility.

We further propose that demand for tokenized outputs may exhibit nonlinear, Jevons-type dynamics, whereby declining costs induce disproportionate increases in consumption. We formalize this mechanism by modeling demand as a power function of token cost, and show that under nonlinear demand, cost reductions may increase total expenditure, challenging conventional deflationary narratives.

This framework suggests that AI-driven price changes are best understood as relative price adjustments rather than generalized economic contraction, offering a new perspective on employment and deflation concerns.

This version (v2) extends the framework by introducing a distinction between token production and token consumption components in the T sector.

title: Time on Your Side: Labor Market Effects of Foreclosure Delays
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Time on Your Side: Labor Market Effects of Foreclosure Delays
detail.abstract: I study how foreclosure delays affect labor income. I exploit a 2021 CFPB servicing rule that restricted servicers from initiating foreclosure on eligible loans, delaying filings by up to four months. Using matched employer–employee payroll records linked to credit files, I estimate a difference-in-differences design comparing borrowers who became 120+ days delinquent one-month before versus one-month after the eligibility cutoff. Eligible borrowers’ incomes rise 2%–2.5%, driven by job switching and moves to higher-paying firms. Effects are larger for liquidity-constrained borrowers and where housing-tenure stability is costly. Realized foreclosures decline in subsequent months, implying short filing safeguards can reduce distress by facilitating labor-market reallocation.

title: AI "Errors"
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and Singapore Management University - Lee Kong Chian School of Business

detail.title: AI "Errors"
detail.abstract: When AIs are tasked with empirical research, how do their outcomes compare to those of humans? Are the distributions similar? We run an experiment where we let AI models repeat an experiment that was run with 164 human teams. Not surprisingly, distributions differ. The deeper question is: Why? We develop an approach that identifies which decisions on the analysis path drive these differences, which we define as "AI errors." The results show that AI concentrates on a narrow set of analysis paths, yielding markedly lower dispersion. For complex tasks, their estimates are systematically shifted relative to the human benchmark. Fork-level diagnostics and quantile regressions trace these shifts primarily to the choice of the statistical model, e.g., identifying a time trend by adding a stationary trend to a model in levels, or by computing relative changes and taking the average.

title: Social Norms 2.0: From Private Governance to Co-evolution
affiliations: Duke University School of Law

detail.title: Social Norms 2.0: From Private Governance to Co-evolution
detail.abstract: This essay engages with Florian Grisel’s The Limits of Private Governance and uses it as a springboard to rethink the theoretical foundations of the social norms and private governance literature. Drawing on Grisel’s historical study of the Prud’homie de pêche of Marseille—a centuries-old institution that governed fisheries—as well as my own research on property and neighborhood governance in China, including Chinese Small Property and The Authoritarian Commons, the essay proposes a new framework: “social norms 2.0.” This approach views governance as a process of co-evolution in which norms, legal institutions, and political authority continuously reshape one another. By reframing private governance as a dynamic and relational process, the co-evolutionary model moves the field beyond conventional debates about whether governance emerges primarily from informal norms or from state support. The essay suggests that future research should focus instead on the recursive interactions through which social norms, legal institutions, and political authority jointly produce and transform systems of governance.

detail.abstract: In classical finance, the risk-return trade-off indicates that more risk should be compensated with higher rewards. However, in Bangladesh's banking sector, an inverse link is observed-the "Risk-Return Paradox." This work expands upon prior research (Shaham, 2026) which revealed that farmers pay greater interest for productive assets (tractors) than urban borrowers for consumption (cars). By evaluating data from 2025-2026 across major commercial banks, this analysis indicates that granular agricultural loans (13%-16%) are priced much more than large corporate loans (9%-12%), despite the latter posing a tremendous Systemic Risk. With the national Non-Performing Loan (NPL) ratio reaching record highs mostly driven by business defaults, this study calls for a paradigm shift in interest rate pricing to maintain economic equality.

title: From Digital Content Creators to Socio-Political Actors: The Rising Influence of Online Personalities on Economic and Political Dynamics in Cameroon
affiliations: Highstone International University, Highstone International University and Charisma University

detail.title: From Digital Content Creators to Socio-Political Actors: The Rising Influence of Online Personalities on Economic and Political Dynamics in Cameroon
detail.abstract: This article examines the rapidly evolving role of digital content creators and social media influencers in Cameroon's economic and political spheres. Drawing on recent policy developments, including the 2026 Finance Law's fiscal reforms targeting digital activities, and analysis of political mobilization patterns during and after the 2025 presidential election, the study argues that Cameroonian influencers have emerged as significant socioeconomic actors whose influence now extends beyond entertainment into domains of taxation policy, political discourse, and geopolitical positioning. The research identifies a fundamental paradox: while Cameroonian influencers face structural barriers to direct platform monetization, their growing visibility has prompted state regulatory responses and positioned them as key players in political mobilization, diaspora engagement, and international influence operations. Through analysis of leaked documents revealing Wagner Group payments totaling approximately $36,000 to Cameroonian and West African influencers in 2022 alone, examination of diaspora-led political mobilization including protests in Germany and the United States, and investigation of alternative economic strategies including cross-border e-commerce, the article proposes the concept of **"visibility without monetization"** to characterize the Cameroonian influencer economy. The study further documents the emergence of what we term **"digital sovereignty deficits"**-the gap between state regulatory ambitions and technical capacity to enforce digital policies. Drawing on documentary analysis, case study investigation, and synthesis of investigative journalism reports, this article presents the first comprehensive mapping of Cameroon's emerging influencer-political complex, with implications for governance, civic participation, and digital sovereignty across the African continent.

title: Credance-based Collateral Exchange

detail.title: Credance-based Collateral Exchange
detail.abstract: This paper introduces Credance-Based Collateral Exchange (CBCE) as a formal category of financial instrument distinct from conventional repo and from existing distributed ledger collateral protocols. Building on the concept of credance-the collective anterior belief that makes a financial transaction possible before any track record exists (Laverriere, 2026)-we argue that a significant class of collateral exchange activity operates on the basis of credance rather than documentation. We formalise credance as a time-varying bilateral function C(P₁, P₂, t), define the credance threshold θ as a composite score of transaction history, temporal depth, and costly honouring, and propose a three-mode typology of CBCE instruments. We analyse the conditions under which each mode is optimal, examine the implications for Islamic repo market development and for distributed ledger technology design, and argue that blockchain-based collateral protocols have systematically failed to incorporate credance as a design variable. A credance-aware DLT architectureincluding a credance oracle, a zero-knowledge credance proof mechanism, and a variable collateralisation ratio governed by C(P₁, P₂, t)-would represent a genuinely novel class of financial instrument. The paper concludes with a research agenda including a call for collaboration between financial economists and DLT researchers to prototype the proposed architecture.

title:
Africa's Growth Paradox: 
Jobless Growth, Informality, and the Rise of the Platform Economy
affiliations: Nobel International Business School

detail.title:
Africa's Growth Paradox: 
Jobless Growth, Informality, and the Rise of the Platform Economy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the structural disconnect between economic growth and decent work outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa. Despite sustained periods of GDP expansion, employment growth has remained insufficient and largely concentrated in informal and vulnerable sectors. Using employment elasticity analysis, macro-labour linkages, and qualitative assessment of labour market dynamics, the study identifies persistent decent work deficits, including high informality, youth unemployment, working poverty, and the rapid emergence of platform-based gig work. The findings demonstrate that Africa’s growth model has been capital-intensive and weakly employment-generating. The rise of the digital platform economy introduces both opportunities and risks, potentially reproducing informal labour relations in technologically mediated forms. The paper argues for a recalibration of growth strategies toward labour-absorbing structural transformation, strengthened social protection systems, and regulatory frameworks that extend decent work standards to platform labour. The analysis calls for integrated macro-labour policy frameworks that align economic expansion with employment intensity, social protection coverage, and inclusive development.

title: The Connectivity between Geopolitical Risks, Uncertainty, Commodity and Cryptocurrency Markets
affiliations: Ondokuz Mayis University

detail.title: The Connectivity between Geopolitical Risks, Uncertainty, Commodity and Cryptocurrency Markets
detail.abstract: The connectivity between geopolitical risks, uncertainty, commodity and cryptocurrency markets Geopolitical risks have continued to affect the economies and various markets by affecting supply chains and causing uncertainties. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the relationships between geopolitical risks, uncertainty, agriculture prices, metal prices, energy prices, and Bitcoin prices using monthly data over June 2012-September 2024. By using connectedness measures and different geopolitical tensions, results show significant relationships between geopolitical risks, uncertainty, commodities, and cryptocurrency. Findings indicate return and volatility spillovers among different markets. Findings indicate the effect of geopolitical risks on the return and volatility of energy transition metals related to the transition to a low-carbon economy. Therefore, necessary steps should be taken immediately to reduce geopolitical tensions and uncertainties, which may impede the low-carbon economy transition and, therefore, may be an obstacle to achieving climate change-related goals.

title: Civic Liberties and Entrepreneurial Outcomes
affiliations: University of Groningen and University of Southampton

detail.title: Civic Liberties and Entrepreneurial Outcomes
detail.abstract: We examine the microfoundations of how free speech protections shape entrepreneurial outcomes. Exploiting staggered adoption and cross-state variation in the strength of U.S. anti-SLAPP statutes between 1990 and 2020, we study their effects on venture formation, financing, innovation, and exit outcomes using data on over 18,000 private firms. Anti-SLAPP laws reduce venture entry by 22% but have no effect on aggregate venture capital investment, IPO activity, or IPO pricing. Bankruptcies and acquisitions decline by 34% and 19%, while treated ventures file significantly more patents. These patterns are consistent with selection effects: stronger speech protections raise the cost of opacity, deter lower-quality entry, and improve screening in private markets. The results suggest that institutional reforms that safeguard civic liberties may augment traditional subsidy-based innovation policies.

title: Financing Rivals
affiliations: and Universidad Andrés Bello

detail.title: Financing Rivals

detail.abstract: We study how a lender with market power shapes competition between liquidityconstrained rivals. In many settings, including innovation races, procurement, and political contests, the same lender may fund competing firms and choose contract terms strategically. We develop a model in which two firms compete for a prize and a monopolistic lender decides which firms to finance and on what terms. We show that the lender finances both rivals when their internal resources are similar, but finances only the more constrained firm when asymmetries are large. When financing both firms, the lender optimally caps credit rather than fully relaxing financial constraints, because full funding induces an inefficient investment arms race that lowers the surplus available for extraction. We also show that, even when the lender can use fees, caps, and interest rates, an optimal contract sets interest rates to zero and relies on non-distortionary instruments instead. Thus, common lenders do not simply supply funds: they act as strategic arbiters of rivalry, and their effect on competition depends critically on the initial distribution of resources.

title: Adaptive Engram Memory System for Indonesian Language Model: Generative AI based on TOBA LM for Batak and Minang Language
affiliations: Bandung Fe Institute, Bandung Fe Institute and Bandung Fe Institute

detail.title: Adaptive Engram Memory System for Indonesian Language Model: Generative AI based on TOBA LM for Batak and Minang Language
detail.abstract: This study presents TOBA-LM, a trilingual language model based on GPT-2 architecture with 1.2 billion parameters, trained on a corpus encompassing Indonesian, Batak, and Minangkabau using syllabic-agglutinative tokenization. The architecture integrates an Engram Memory mechanism, an adaptive n-gram-based memory system with a 500,000 × 768 embedding table that captures morphological dependencies through bigram and trigram pathways. Empirical results demonstrate a training efficiency of 80%, with the loss value dropping from 6.4 to 1.7996 in only 12,973 steps-significantly faster than the conventional transformer architecture, which required over 70,000 steps to achieve comparable convergence. These findings confirm that the integration of external statistical memory substantially reduces computational requirements for developing regional language models under limited resources.

title: Why Dark Pools Fail: A Dynamic Model of Liquidity, Adverse Selection, and Fee Design in Japan's PTS Ecosystem

detail.title: Why Dark Pools Fail: A Dynamic Model of Liquidity, Adverse Selection, and Fee Design in Japan's PTS Ecosystem

keywords: Dark Pools and Alternative Trading Systems

detail.abstract: Dark pools frequently fail soon after launch, while a small number achieve durable liquidity. This paper develops a dynamic model of dark pool economics calibrated to the Japanese equity market. The model combines a heterogeneous trader population, a logistic replicator migration dynamic, adverse selection feedback, and revenue-optimal fee design within a single tractable framework applied to proprietary trading system (PTS) launch. We study liquidity migration between a lit exchange and a dark pool, deriving a closed-form migration fraction under logistic urgency whose monotonicity in pool liquidity, fee, and non-execution penalty is verified by Mathematica symbolic computation. Equilibrium structure is governed by a saddle-node bifurcation in the churn rate γ: for γ below a critical value γ c , a thin-pool saddle and a thickpool attractor coexist, implying that the PTS operator must seed the pool above a minimum threshold to escape the thin-pool trap. Adverse selection introduces a second feedback loop that compresses the viable operating region in (γ, κ) parameter space; a critical adverse selection intensity κ c exists above which the pool always fails regardless of initial conditions. The optimal dark pool fee satisfies an inverse elasticity rule with no closed-form solution; numerical calibration to Japan equity market parameters yields f * D ≈ 0.91 yen/share and annual revenue R * ≈ ¥ 52M at approximately 23.5% flow migration.

title: Range Wars and their Resolution: A Spatial Model with Experimental Evidence
affiliations: and Chapman University - Smith Institute for Political Economy and Philosophy

detail.title: Range Wars and their Resolution: A Spatial Model with Experimental Evidence
detail.abstract: We develop a spatial model of range conflict in which resource concentration determines the extent of territorial overlap in equilibrium. We then test the model's predictions and two resolution mechanisms: self-coordination and decentralized exchange, in a virtual laboratory experiment. Resource concentration affects range overlap as the model predicts: more concentrated resources lead to less overlap in absolute terms but more overlap in percentage terms. Decentralized exchange substantially reduces conflict relative to self-coordination across all resource environments and group sizes, though many groups do not fully resolve their disputes even with the ability to communicate and transfer money. Together, these findings illuminate the economic origins of territorial conflict and establish decentralized exchange as a promising, if imperfect, tool for pre-conflict resolution.

title: Political Turnover and Corporate Cash Holdings: Evidence from Close Mayoral Elections
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: Political Turnover and Corporate Cash Holdings: Evidence from Close Mayoral Elections
detail.abstract: We estimate the causal effect of municipal political turnover on corporate cash holdings using a regression discontinuity design applied to 2,397 U.S. mayoral elections (1992-2022). Firms in municipal-dependent industries-construction, transportation and utilities, and health and social services-increase their cash-to-assets ratio by 5.5 percentage points (p = 0.0002) in the fiscal year of an incumbent's narrow defeat, strengthening to 7.3 percentage points with covariate adjustment. The effect is absent in the general population of firms and in industries dependent on federal rather than municipal government, confirming that the transmission operates through local policy channels. The cash increase fully reverses within one fiscal year. Three mechanism tests distinguish post-election policy uncertainty from anticipatory precautionary saving: (i) a difference-indifferences comparison finds no pre-election cash buildup in election cities relative to non-election cities (p = 0.68); (ii) cumulative abnormal stock returns are significantly negative when the incumbent barely loses (-0.117, p = 0.029); and (iii) the effect is identical in cities with frequent mayoral turnover and those without, indicating that firms respond to uncertainty about what the new mayor will do, not the surprise of turnover itself.

title: DMA Innovation
affiliations: University of Zurich - Institute of Law

detail.title: DMA Innovation
detail.abstract: In a challenging global environment, the EU is intensely debating its competitiveness and innovativeness. An endeavour to improve its performance in these respects must include a critical review of key elements of the Union's legal framework, with the GDPR and the recent, or impending, "Digital Acts"-Data Act, DSA, DGA, DMA, AI Act-taking centre stage. These Acts regulate digital business models and frontier technologies, viz. subjects for which, inter alia, the Draghi Report has diagnosed particular relevance to, and deficits in, the EU's global competitiveness. Against this background, but also in the context of its first regular evaluation due in May 2026, the present contribution attempts to take initial stock of how the Digital Markets Act performs on innovation. It approaches this complex topic from several perspectives by reflecting on what "innovation" means in the first place and how the DMA, and pertinent examples from EU law more generally, frame this concept; surveying relevant, DMA-specific empirical data available to date; discussing case law originating from the enforcement of both the DMA and general EU competition law; asking how innovation-related findings in these cases interact towards a guiding concept for DMA enforcement; analysing how key DMA provisions could be retrofitted for the Gatekeepers' evolving business activities in the field of artificial intelligence ("A"); and summarizing the results in theses. Far from claiming comprehensiveness, these perspectives indicate that there are two sides of the coin to "DMA innovation", namely the Act's current impact on the innovativeness of EU markets and modifications to the DMA which may help to optimize said impact.

By synthesizing the realism of Machiavelli, the deception of Sun Tzu, and the cold statecraft of Chanakya, we identify the "Qadisiyyah Protocol": a strategic alignment where Arab monarchies have successfully baited their 1,400-year rival into a war of total liquidation, utilizing Western capital and Israeli security as the primary instruments of execution.

detail.title: Workforce Mobility and Labor Market Stability: Reframing Employer Compliance Systems as Economic Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Workforce mobility is a critical determinant of labor market efficiency, economic productivity, and institutional resilience. However, the effectiveness of workforce mobility is significantly influenced by the strength and structure of employer compliance systems, which govern employment authorization, regulatory compliance, payroll reporting, and workforce onboarding.

title: Insider Trading Reform and Market Quality: Evidence from the 2023 Rule 10b5-1 Amendments
affiliations: State University of New York at Buffalo - School of Management and Kansas State University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Insider Trading Reform and Market Quality: Evidence from the 2023 Rule 10b5-1 Amendments
detail.abstract: We analyze the market impact of the SEC’s 2023 amendments to Rule 10b5-1, which introduced cooling-off periods, restrictions on overlapping plans, and enhanced disclosure requirements. We show that insider trading decreases significantly after the reform, particularly among firms with high insider trading levels prior to the amendments. Simultaneously, price impact, quoted spreads, and effective spreads decrease, market depths increase, and price efficiency improves. Instrumental-variable estimates confirm that declines in insider trading lead to better liquidity and efficiency. The evidence indicates that the amendments significantly reduced opportunistic insider trading and improved overall market quality.

title: Cryptographically Auditable Decision Governance for Autonomous Trading Systems: A Production Study OMNIX Quantum

detail.title: Cryptographically Auditable Decision Governance for Autonomous Trading Systems: A Production Study OMNIX Quantum

detail.abstract: We present a production deployment of a fail-closed decision governance framework for autonomous trading systems, combining a six-checkpoint evaluation pipeline with post-quantum cryptographic audit trails. Over 49 days of continuous operation, the system processed 693,890 evaluation cycles and generated 27,449 governance receipts, each cryptographically signed using Dilithium-3 (NIST-standardized ML-DSA-65) and linked into a SHA-256 hash chain providing tamper-evident provenance. Unlike prior governance frameworks that operate as post-hoc compliance layers, our architecture enforces governance at decision time: any gate failure produces an immediate BLOCKED outcome with no override path. The system is domain-agnostic-the same six-checkpoint pipeline has been validated for trading signals and extended via a REST API to credit and insurance domains. All receipts are publicly verifiable without access to internal systems. To our knowledge, this is the first reported production deployment of post-quantum cryptographic governance receipts for autonomous decision systems.

title: Carbon Price Shocks and Stock Market Reactions
affiliations: Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg and Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg

detail.title: Carbon Price Shocks and Stock Market Reactions
detail.abstract: We examine whether carbon allowance prices under the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) are reflected in stock prices. Using installation-level data from 2008 to 2024 mapped to the firm level, we construct shortfall intensity, defined as the number of allowances a firm must purchase scaled by firm revenues, to measure firms' economic exposure to the EU ETS. Analyzing both the relationship between carbon price changes and stock returns as well as stock market reactions to carbon price shocks, we find that the association varies across EU ETS phases and turns negative and significant for regulated firms in Phase IV. Thus, positive carbon price changes are associated with negative stock returns for firms that must use a larger portion of their revenues to purchase allowances, and vice versa. For unregulated firms, we also document a negative association, consistent with spillover effects and exposure to regulatory risk. Overall, while statistically significant, the economic magnitude of the effects remains small.

title: Structure and Determinants of Green and Non-Green Global Innovation Networks: Evidence from Global Patent Data
affiliations: University of Pisa - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Structure and Determinants of Green and Non-Green Global Innovation Networks: Evidence from Global Patent Data
detail.abstract: This article compares the structure and determinants of green and non-green global innovation networks using 287,388 collaborative patents filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) between 1991 and 2020. Drawing on social network analysis, the study shows that both networks exhibit similar macro-level structural patterns, characterised by persistent coreperiphery configurations and high levels of network centralisation. Count-based exponential random graph models (ERGMs) indicate that the drivers of cross-border co-invention are largely common across domains. Technological proximity, shared language, economic complexity, and economic size consistently emerge as the strongest predictors of collaboration, while trade flows and geographic distance exert more modest effects. Environmental conditions play a more limited role: higher pollution levels are associated with lower participation in green collaboration, whereas greater deployment of renewable energy correlates with increased engagement. Overall, the findings suggest that green innovation networks remain conditioned by pre-existing technological capabilities and embedded within the structural logic that shapes global innovation networks more broadly.

title: Employer-Side Immigration Compliance In The Us: Designing Structured Sponsorship Governance Systems For Workforce Mobility

detail.title: Employer-Side Immigration Compliance In The Us: Designing Structured Sponsorship Governance Systems For Workforce Mobility
detail.abstract: Employer-sponsored immigration plays a critical role in facilitating workforce mobility and addressing labor market needs in the United States. Organizations increasingly rely on foreign professionals to fill skill shortages in sectors such as technology, healthcare, and engineering. However, employer participation in employment-based immigration programs involves complex regulatory obligations administered by multiple federal agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, and the Department of Labor. These obligations include employment eligibility verification, labor certification requirements, wage compliance, and documentation management. Despite the importance of these regulatory responsibilities, many organizations manage immigration sponsorship processes through fragmented administrative systems that lack structured governance and compliance oversight. This study examines employer-side immigration compliance through the lens of organizational governance and regulatory risk management. Drawing on migration governance scholarship, corporate governance theory, and regulatory compliance frameworks, the research analyzes the institutional challenges organizations face in managing immigration sponsorship programs. The study proposes a Structured Sponsorship Governance Model (SSGM) designed to integrate executive oversight, compliance management systems, legal review mechanisms, human resource coordination, and digital immigration case management infrastructure. Using qualitative policy analysis and a comprehensive review of migration policy literature, the study demonstrates how structured governance systems can strengthen employer compliance with immigration regulations while supporting workforce mobility and global talent management

title: Section 131(5) of the Companies Act 1993: A Problem of Lack of Accountability

detail.title: Section 131(5) of the Companies Act 1993: A Problem of Lack of Accountability

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Auckland Faculty of Law Research Paper Series (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: The University of Auckland Faculty of Law Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This article discusses whether s 131(5) of the Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand) adversely impacts on the accountability of directors. Section 131(1) sets out the fundamental duty of directors to act in the best interests of the company. Section 131(5) provides that “in considering the best interests of a company … a director may consider matters other than the maximisation of profit (for example, environmental, social and governance matters)”. The article suggests that s 131(5) will not improve the position of the environment, or of other stakeholders other than the directors themselves (who will have a better ability to mask self‑interested transactions). The proper implementation of social reform requires specific and detailed legislation or regulation binding on all businesses, including but not limited to companies. The article concludes that s 131(5) will, if retained, make directors less accountable. It will allow directors to more readily justify any decisions they wish to take (including decisions motivated by self-interest) based on some claimed environmental, social and governance matter. As such,s 131(5) will destroy director accountability and give directors ample opportunity to camouflage decisions taken in their own self-interest without fear of adverse consequences.

This article was first published by Thomson Reuters New Zealand in the New Zealand Business Law Quarterly and should be cited as:

• John Land “Section 131(5) of the Companies Act 1993: A Problem of Lack of Accountability” (2025) 28 NZBLQ 53.

title: Political and Institutional Development in England
affiliations: George Mason University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Political and Institutional Development in England

declarations.funderStatement: am grateful for external funding from the Mercatus Center's Pluralism \& Exchange Grant, an Emergent Ventures grant, and The John Templeton Foundation (Grant 62593)

detail.abstract: This paper revisits the political and institutional development of England from the Magna Carta to the Glorious Revolution. I argue that institutional change in this period is best understood through the lens of coalition formation. Political elites had heterogeneous preferences over first two, and then three, recurring axes of disagreement: constitutional prerogatives, foreign policy, and after the Reformation, religion. Institutional change occurred when shocks caused coalitions to form, fracture, and realign. I discuss three episodes. First, due to defeat in France, a baronial coalition was able to check the power of the king through the Magna Carta. Second, the Reformation introduced religion as a new axis of conflict, ultimately giving rise to organised political parties during the Exclusion Crisis of 1679-1681. Third, the Glorious Revolution succeeded when James II's pro-Catholic policies shattered the Tory coalition that had sustained the late. Stuart monarchy. Using data on 750 Exclusion Crisis MPs, I document the structure of these political alignments empirically, and discuss how the defection of Tory elites was decisive in 1688.

title: Education in Yemen during the Armed Conflict: The Impact of Teachers' Salary Interruptions on the Quality of Education
affiliations: Sakarya University

detail.title: Education in Yemen during the Armed Conflict: The Impact of Teachers' Salary Interruptions on the Quality of Education
detail.abstract: This research examines the impact of teacher salary cuts in Yemen during the armed conflict on the quality of the educational process, as one of the most important structural factors that contributed to the deterioration of the educational system during the years of conflict. Since 2015, the Yemeni education sector has faced overlapping challenges of infrastructure destruction, institutional breakdowns, mass displacement of teachers and students, as well as the near-complete or irregular payment of teachers' salaries. The research relies on a descriptive-analytical approach through a review of scientific literature, peer-reviewed studies, and reports from relevant international organizations. The results of the analysis show that the interruption of salaries directly contributed to the decline in the professional motivation of teachers, the decline in job stability, the high rates of absenteeism and dropout, in addition to the low levels of academic achievement of students. The research concludes that ensuring regular teachers' salaries is an essential input to improve the quality of education and rebuild human capital in Yemen.

detail.abstract: We develop Structured-Knowledge-Informed Neural Networks (SKINNs), a unified estimation framework that embeds theoretical, simulated, previously learned, or cross-domain insights as differentiable constraints within flexible neural function approximation. SKINNs jointly estimate neural network parameters and economically meaningful structural parameters in a single optimization problem, enforcing theoretical consistency not only on observed data but over a broader input domain through collocation, and therefore nesting approaches such as functional GMM, Bayesian updating, transfer learning, PINNs, and surrogate modeling. SKINNs define a class of M-estimators that are consistent and asymptotically normal with √ N convergence, sandwich covariance, and recovery of pseudo-true parameters under misspecification. We establish identification of structural parameters under joint flexibility, derive generalization and target-risk bounds under distributional shift in a convex proxy, and provide a restricted-optimal characterization of the weighting parameter that governs the bias-variance tradeoff. In an illustrative financial application to option pricing, SKINNs improve out-of-sample valuation and hedging performance, particularly at longer horizons and during high-volatility regimes, while recovering economically interpretable structural parameters with improved stability relative to conventional calibration. More broadly, SKINNs provide a general econometric framework for combining model-based reasoning with high-dimensional, data-driven estimation.

detail.abstract: Declining fertility and population loss pose significant challenges for state and federal local governments responsible for providing a range of services to citizens, including education, health care, and infrastructure. Indeed, many areas are already experiencing outright population decline, with roughly half of U.S. counties losing population between 2010 and 2020. This paper examines how shrinking and aging populations affect the operations and fiscal sustainability of state and local governments. Preliminary evidence presented in this paper suggests that scaling down educational services is considerably more difficult than scaling up. The estimated per-enrollee cost increases associated with a 10 percent enrollment decline are four times larger than the cost decreases associated with a 10 percent enrollment increase. Regions with contracting populations will face additional challenges as a smaller working-age population bears the burden of funding pensions and retiree health plans for larger aging cohorts. While lower fertility can create a short run fiscal dividend as local governments serve fewer children, that dividend will only be realized if state and local public officials make efficient retrenchment a priority.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Aspen Economic Strategy Group Policy Paper Series No. 2

detail.abstract: The discussion of impending population decline is often dismissed or minimized by arguments that downplay its urgency – or even welcome this development – because of the proposed environmental benefits. This paper argues that the environmental benefits of depopulation are far smaller than widely believed, and that complacency about population decline may be counterproductive to climate goals. First, there is a fundamental issue of timing mismatch. Demographic change unfolds over generations, while effective responses to emissions and environmental harm require immediate action. Second, effective climate strategies, such as carbon capture, require high fixed capital and labor costs. The smaller the economy, the larger the share of national income required to achieve climate goals. Beyond the climate, there is little evidence to suggest that increases in per-capita resource availability from depopulation would materially improve living standards, as modern natural-resource constraints on well-being are limited and declining. In contrast, sustainability depends on policy, human ingenuity, and fiscal capacity, none of which are aided by a shrinking and aging population. Taken together, this paper argues that effective sustainability policy will require sustained public investment and proactive policy.

title: Landsat phenology and machine learning enables sub-field corn yield mapping at 30-meter resolution
affiliations: University of Arkansas, University of Texas at Austin, U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Landsat phenology and machine learning enables sub-field corn yield mapping at 30-meter resolution
detail.abstract: Yield prediction is critical for agricultural production, but accurate estimates over large areas remain difficult. Remote sensing enables spatially continuous predictions, yet many existing methods rely on county-level statistics that may obscure sub-county spatiotemporal patterns. Here we applied machine learning to predict corn (Zea mays L.) yield at sub-field resolution (30 × 30 m2) by pairing a large yield monitor dataset (n=62 field-years) with Landsat satellite imagery. Our objective was to develop a robust method based solely on Landsat-derived phenology metrics and spectral vegetation indices capturing canopy greenness, moisture content, and senescence. Using data from 2007–2019 across eight U.S. states, we trained models achieving high accuracy (R2=0.82, RMSE=1.23 Mg ha−1), improving upon previous Landsat-based models by ~16%. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) revealed that higher canopy moisture and earlier start of season were the strongest predictors of high yield. We then scaled predictions to the county level and validated against NASS survey data; counties with substantial corn production (>1,000 ha) showed strong agreement (R2=0.71, RMSE=1.84 Mg ha−1). Results demonstrate the predictive power of spectrally derived vegetative and phenological properties, while our interpretable ML approach suggested earlier emergence and higher moisture may improve yield outcomes. This method offers potential for spatially continuous yield mapping to inform precision management, improve forecasting, and advance understanding of environmental controls on crop production.

title: Arts Tax Policy: Democracy or Plutocracy?

detail.title: Arts Tax Policy: Democracy or Plutocracy?

detail.abstract: The United States National Endowment for the Arts' budget in 2024 was $207 million; in the same year the United States spent roughly between $2 and $3.35 billion on art through the charitable contribution deduction. Over 90% of those deductions came from people earning more than $200,000, while 65% came from those earning more than $1,000,000. Is there justification for Congress to provide charitable tax benefits including tax exemption to support arts-based nonprofit organizations this way? This Article finds no theory of justice supports this policy as currently designed. Though tax scholars typically consider factors of efficiency or equity, neither resolves this question. We need a theory of political justice. The charitable tax subsidies fail because no theory justifies allowing wealthy interests the primary say in what art the country supports, and because the current design is unlikely to fix any market failure. Underlying both failures is the neutrality principle of liberal democracy: the state should not privilege one form of the good life over another. This is a principle the tax literature has largely ignored. Though art can serve genuine democratic purposes by developing the reflective and communicative capacities citizens need for self-governance, that case requires art policy to be determined through inclusive democratic deliberation rather than wealthy donor preferences. Judged against the standard of democratic perfectionism, the current structure substitutes plutocracy for democracy in a domain where democratic deliberation is what political justice requires.

title: Marketing to Machines: How AI Models Respond to Promotional Cues
affiliations: and King's College London

detail.abstract: As AI agents increasingly make purchasing decisions on behalf of consumers, do standard promotional cues designed for human cognition retain their influence? We examine whether common promotional cues designed to influence human shoppers affect AI models in comparable ways. We develop a controlled simulation environment that replicates common e-commerce promotional badges—including assurance signals, scarcity, strike-through pricing, countdown timers, social proof, vouchers, bundles, and ratings—and conduct repeated simulated choice experiments using four widely deployed AI models across four product categories. The results reveal pronounced heterogeneity both across models and across product categories within the same model. Among the badges tested, only ratings consistently increased selection probabilities across models in a manner aligned with established human reliance on quality signals. All other promotional effects varied by model and product category. In an exploratory follow-up, we examined whether these patterns could be explained by human behavioural mechanisms or instead reflected model-specific computational responses. Constructs derived from prospect theory, including loss aversion, probability weighting, and diminishing sensitivity, provided little systematic explanatory power. These findings show that AI models cannot be treated as a homogeneous class of decision-makers, and offer insight into how AI agents may behave in real e-commerce settings. More broadly, they suggest that marketing-to-machines cannot be inferred directly from established human behavioural theory. The study offers practical implications for platforms, merchants, and AI developers as algorithmic intermediaries play an expanding role in online purchasing decisions.

detail.abstract: Recent years witnessed shareholder activism being instrumental in shaping corporations' sustainability adoption along with ethics and productivity improvement. The global climate change phenomenon necessitates firms to focus on sustainable business management practices which in turn helps firms to address environmental, social and governance issues. This study examines how shareholder activism influences ESG performance in Indian banks between 2020 and 2024. Using a stakeholder engagement framework, it explores how institutional investor proposals, proxy voting outcomes, and regulatory pressures impact sustainability efforts across governance, environmental, and social dimensions. Data was collected through ESG score databases, SEBI and RBI disclosures, and a qualitative review of annual and sustainability reports from major Indian banks. Analysis using panel data regression and thematic content analysis reveals that higher institutional engagement and favourable voting outcomes are associated with stronger ESG practices, particularly in governance and social responsibility. The findings offer investors, regulators, and banks strategic insights to align shareholder influence with sustainability goals in India's evolving ESG and regulatory landscape.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how relationship banking shapes firms' environmental investment decisions. Combining plant-level data on green investments with bank-firm relationship records for French manufacturers, we exploit the 2016 French floods as an exogenous shock to environmental awareness. Our difference-indifferences estimates show that long-term banking ties reduce the likelihood of investing in pollution prevention when firms are more dependent on their main lenders. This pattern reflects the transformative and unconventional nature of these investments, which may challenge banks' accumulated informational capital, particularly when the scale of the required environmental transition is substantial.

title: Exports Composition And Economic Growth In Uganda

detail.title: Exports Composition And Economic Growth In Uganda
detail.abstract:
The study aimed at establishing the type of exports that lead to economic growth in Uganda. Specifically, it aimed at establishing the effect of traditional and non-traditional exports on economic growth. It was based on time series annual data from 1989 to 2018 obtained from Uganda Bureau of Statistics and World Bank Development Indicators. The study was based on the Auto Regressive distributed Lag Model (ARDL)for estimating empirical results.

The results show that in Uganda’s case, it is non-traditional exports and traditional exports that lead to economic growth. Other important variables influencing economic growth include the conventional factors of production that’s gross capital formation and labor force participation rate, in addition to civil liberties index.

The study recommends that government should strongly strategize in promoting value addition to agricultural products like fish and fish products, petroleum products, sugar, and many more (non-traditional exports) so these products are able to compete internationally in terms of quality and prices. Additionally, the government should strategize to improve the manufacturing exports as it would be important for Uganda’s long-term development.

detail.title:
Account-based Marketing 
In the Era of Strategic Intelligence
detail.abstract:
B2B purchase decisions have undergone a structural transformation. 

Where convincing a single procurement manager once sufficed, today every buying decision involves an average of six to ten stakeholders, each with distinct objectives, concerns, and success metrics (Gartner, 2019-2024). This complexity has rendered standardised sales strategies obsolete and opened a decisive competitive space for those who know how to orchestrate personalised conversations with complex decision-making ecosystems. 

This paper argues that Account-Based Marketing (ABM)-when integrated with a strategic intelligence logic and targeted thought leadership-represents the most effective response to this complexity. ABM is not a lead generation tactic but a paradigm shift: from mass marketing to the surgical conquest of high-value accounts, one account and one stakeholder at a time. 

We propose the Applied Strategic Intelligence (ASI) framework, which describes how the collection, interpretation, and activation of contextual data on target accounts — combined with thought leadership content calibrated to their strategic imperatives — generates sustainable competitive advantage in high-complexity B2B environments. The paper includes a case study from the cybersecurity/banking sector and specific implications for Italian industrial SMEs.

title: Lifecycle Tracking Models For Employment-Based Visa Sponsorship In Multi-Entity U.S. Organizations

detail.title: Lifecycle Tracking Models For Employment-Based Visa Sponsorship In Multi-Entity U.S. Organizations
detail.abstract: Employment-based visa sponsorship in the United States is a complex, multi-stage process that requires continuous compliance with evolving regulatory requirements. In multi-entity organizations, this complexity is amplified by decentralized structures, fragmented data management, and limited integration between immigration processes and enterprise systems. This study addresses these challenges by proposing a lifecycle-based tracking model for managing employment-based visa sponsorship within multi-entity U.S. organizations. Adopting a conceptual and systems design methodology, the study integrates insights from immigration policy, organizational theory, and information systems to develop a structured framework that aligns visa sponsorship processes with enterprise system architecture. The proposed model conceptualizes visa sponsorship as a continuous lifecycle, encompassing initiation, petitioning, monitoring, renewal, transition, and closure stages. It further emphasizes the integration of immigration compliance into Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Human Resource Information Systems (HRIS) to enable centralized data management, automated workflows, and real-time monitoring. The study draws on Institutional Theory, Systems Theory, and Compliance/Risk Management Theory to explain the need for system-driven approaches to immigration compliance. Findings indicate that existing organizational practices are largely fragmented and reactive, increasing the risk of compliance failures, workforce disruptions, and operational inefficiencies. The proposed lifecycle-based tracking model addresses these gaps by enhancing compliance management capabilities, improving workforce stability, and supporting organizational efficiency.

detail.abstract: We seek to reset the national conversation about poverty by dispelling persistent myths and defining a clear, evidence-based agenda for alleviation. Over the past four decades, poverty in America has fallen markedly, and anti-poverty policies have significantly improved the material well-being of vulnerable households. We document these gains using appropriately constructed measures of income, earnings, and consumption poverty, and other indicators of material conditions. We also describe evidence showing that major programs have improved long-term outcomes for poor children, helping to break intergenerational cycles of poverty. Yet much work remains. We reject the simplistic view that cash transfers alone can solve poverty. While income support is vital, such an approach fails to address poverty’s deeper roots. To confront the complexity of poverty, we propose an agenda centered on equipping people to thrive—by strengthening their skills, building strong families, removing individual barriers to flourishing, and boosting mobility for children born into poverty. These priorities reflect the best available evidence of what works to empower people to provide for themselves and their families and to enable upward mobility and long-term self-sufficiency.

title: Beyond Equilibrium and Disequilibrium: Distributed Valuation Architectures in Monetary Economies
affiliations: Universidad de Alcalá

detail.title: Beyond Equilibrium and Disequilibrium: Distributed Valuation Architectures in Monetary Economies
detail.abstract: Modern monetary economies rarely operate in anything resembling full equilibrium, yet they do not normally collapse into generalized disorder. This article argues that the conventional equilibrium-disequilibrium divide is too coarse to describe that intermediate condition. I propose a meso-theoretical framework in which monetary economies are understood as distributed valuation architectures: multilayer systems in which prices and quasi-prices compress heterogeneous constraints into operational signals that connect productive, distributive, financial, asset, and institutional layers. Within this framework, macroeconomic stability is defined not primarily by market-clearing consistency, but by operative compatibility, namely the capacity of the architecture to preserve functional connectivity under persistent local misalignment. The article introduces the related concepts of recursive tenacity and compatibility failure, models liquidity, rollover, and survival constraints as constitutive mechanisms of monetary buffering, and develops a formal representation in which compatibility is summarized by a non-tautological composite index built from normalized observables and component-specific floors. Within a tractable four-layer specification, the article derives analytical propositions showing that cascade severity depends on Katz centrality in the cross-layer network, that stronger coupling shrinks the region of operative compatibility, that buffer heterogeneity widens the tenacity corridor, that systemic stability requires the spectral radius of the transmission matrix to remain below one, and that credit accommodation improves short-run compatibility while narrowing future resilience. It then outlines a parsimonious computational research design built around an archetypal energy shock to show how centrality, cross-layer coupling, liquidity conditions, and reaction synchronization should affect the transition from resilient adjustment to systemic fragility. The framework offers a disciplined bridge between structural macroeconomics, disequilibrium analysis, monetary theory, and agent-based approaches, while opening a tractable agenda for the study of resilience, contagion, and the changing ecology of valuation.
