detail.abstract: Global maritime transport networks underpin international trade but remain highly vulnerable to operational disruptions that propagate across major trade corridors. Existing resilience assessments primarily rely on static network topology, which measures structural connectivity but provides limited insight into how rapidly cargo flows recover following disturbances. This paper introduces trade viscosity as a dynamic metric capturing the operational frictions that delay cargo reallocation within maritime transport corridors. Container throughput is modeled as a stochastic transport process governed by a Langevin-type differential equation in which recovery dynamics are characterized by a relaxation time parameter. Within this framework, trade viscosity emerges as the friction regulating the speed of flow adjustment toward equilibrium. We further derive an analytical relationship linking steadystate throughput variance to corridor recovery capacity, allowing viscosity to be inferred from observable operational data. Stylized numerical experiments demonstrate that disruption costs scale nonlinearly with trade viscosity. Corridors with high internal friction exhibit prolonged recovery trajectories and disproportionately large cumulative cargo losses following identical shocks. A resilience phasediagram analysis further shows that market volatility amplifies disruption persistence primarily in high-viscosity environments. These results suggest that maritime transport resilience depends not only on network connectivity but also on the dynamic adjustment properties of trade corridors. The proposed framework provides a tractable analytical tool for diagnosing hidden fragility and evaluating resilience-enhancing interventions in global shipping systems.

detail.abstract: US households face unprecedented challenges related to the high cost of housing. In this paper, we characterize the affordability crisis, assess the primary drivers of unaffordable housing, and offer potential policy solutions. We argue that several distinct housing-market challenges—including financing gaps, local restrictions that make it difficult and/or costly to build, and a lack of an entitlement program— present distinct challenges to both an adequate and an affordable housing supply. Importantly, though, the impact of these features becomes more dramatic during economic downturns. Our current national housing challenges are a product of longstanding structural challenges that were amplified by an unprecedented lack of building after the 2008 financial crisis. As a result, the policy recommendations sit within a broader series of reforms and policy solutions that ensure that housing supply meets demand, and that affordability is not compromised, during all periods of the economic cycle.

detail.abstract: The United States’ energy strategy must bridge economic policy and geopolitical power, while offering a calibrated response to climate change. While the country experienced two decades of relatively constant energy consumption, it now faces a surge in power demand driven by artificial intelligence, domestic manufacturing, and continued electrification. These developments challenge an already-constrained domestic electricity grid with limited spare capacity. This paper argues that a renewed strategy should motivate new action to increase energy supply, build infrastructure, and approach greenhouse-gas emissions reductions with competition in mind. Appropriate actions include expanding the development and deployment of nuclear energy, investing in improvements to the high-voltage interstate transmission system, building new natural-gas plants capable of being later retrofitted with carbon capture equipment, and establishing rigorous carbon-accounting standards.

title: Tractable Identification of Strategic Network Formation Models with Unobserved Heterogeneity
affiliations: , University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Tractable Identification of Strategic Network Formation Models with Unobserved Heterogeneity
detail.abstract: We develop a tractable identification approach for strategic network formation models with both strategic link interdependence and individual unobserved heterogeneity (fixed effects). The key challenge is that endogenous network statistics (e.g. number of common friends) enter the link formation equation, while the mapping from model primitives to equilibrium network structure is generally intractable. Our approach sidesteps this difficulty using a "bounding-by-c" technique that treats endogenous covariates as random variables and exploits monotonicity restrictions to obtain identifying information. We derive a system of identifying restrictions based on subnetwork configurations: tetrad-based restrictions that completely eliminate all individual fixed effects, triad-based restrictions that partially difference out fixed effects, and general weighted cycle-based restrictions, along with point identification results. Preliminary simulations show that our approach can deliver informative bounds on the structural parameters.

title: Innovative Entrepreneurs Replace Despair with Hope

detail.title: Innovative Entrepreneurs Replace Despair with Hope

detail.abstract: In the bourgeoise deal the worst off do not begrudge the prosperity of the well off because they hope eventually to earn their own prosperity.  But that hope wavered when regulations limited the ability of innovative entrepreneurs to create new jobs for the worst off.  If deregulated, the innovative entrepreneurs can again create a labor market where a low-skilled worker can usually find a job that gives him hope for a better future.  I reject the common belief that new technology and outsourcing are the causes of the dearth of jobs for the worst off.  Many examples show that innovative entrepreneurs have the desire and ability to find productive uses for the unused, both unused natural resources and unused labor.  When left unbound, innovative entrepreneurs have the means and motivation to find productive employment for unused resources, employing milkweed to insulate parkas or employing desperate small farmers as steel workers to run a new kind of steel mill.  Innovative entrepreneur Ken Iverson at Nucor provides a proof-of-concept that the worst off can benefit when lighter regulation allows innovative entrepreneurs to create more jobs.  Redundant labor markets once flourished before innovative entrepreneurs were heavily regulated.  But several studies show that regulations now restrict the innovative entrepreneur's ability to find uses for the unused.  Beyond deregulating innovative entrepreneurs, the prospects of the worst off also would benefit from the worst off embracing a work ethic, and from deregulation of healthcare.  Some evidence suggests an increasing political openness to systematic deregulation; indicating that the previously politically infeasible, may be becoming feasible.  I conclude by expressing rational optimism, based on past episodes of entrepreneurial liberation, that the worst off will regain hope when innovators are freed.

detail.abstract: Contemporary intellectual property (IP) systems are built on a narrow conceptualisation of knowledge as discrete, codifiable outputs that can be owned, protected, and transferred. While effective in domains where knowledge can be stabilised into artefacts, this model does not generalise across the full spectrum of contemporary research and innovation-particularly in interdisciplinary, practice-based, and socially-oriented fields. The Ambitious Australia Report (2025) identifies university IP policy as overly complex, risk-averse, and commercially disconnected, but does not provide a diagnostic framework for reform. This paper responds directly to that gap. I introduce the proposition that IP systems are downstream expressions of epistemic architecture: they determine not only how knowledge is owned, but which forms of knowledge can be recognised, stabilised, and valued. Drawing on theories of tacit and embodied knowledge (Polanyi, 1966; Nonaka and Takeuchi, 1995; Collins, 2012), appropriability regimes (Teece, 1986), and the political economy of academic knowledge production (Slaughter and Rhoades, 2009), I propose a five-part analytical architecture-Type, Locus, Flow, Intent, Instrument-the TLFII framework. I show that misalignment across any of these five dimensions predicts specific forms of IP failure. The paper introduces a typology of knowledge migration pathways, a strategic intent matrix, and a governance proposition. It identifies a structural market failure-the private developer / public buyer asymmetry-for which current IP frameworks provide no adequate instrument, and proposes a performing rights licensing model, adapted from the creative industries, as a structural solution.

title: "Private" Governance Is Actually a Club Good
affiliations: University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law

detail.title: "Private" Governance Is Actually a Club Good
detail.abstract: Network governance is a club good. Courts that displace a network’s authority to ostracize rule-breakers weaken the excludability that makes governance valuable to members and non-members alike. When the ostracism mechanism loses credibility, members defect from governance obligations, governance quality declines, and the positive externalities governance creates for non-members disappear. Courts should therefore recognize doctrines that defer to network decisions as implicit Pigouvian subsidies that reduce governance costs and help prevent the undersupply of socially valuable governance.

title: Crosstagion: The GENIUS Act, CLARITY, and the OCC-CFTC-SEC Gap in Bidirectional Stablecoin Contagion
affiliations: University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law

detail.title: Crosstagion: The GENIUS Act, CLARITY, and the OCC-CFTC-SEC Gap in Bidirectional Stablecoin Contagion
detail.abstract: The GENIUS Act's prudential framework protects against systemic risk that flows in one direction: from stablecoin failure into traditional banking risk. The empirical record of crosstagion, the bidirectional contagion between traditional finance and decentralized finance, demonstrates that the transmission channel runs the other way as well. When traditional financial stress destabilizes payment stablecoin reserves, as occurred when Silicon Valley Bank's failure briefly unpegged USD Coin in March 2023, the cascade into decentralized markets falls into a jurisdictional gap that neither GENIUS nor the CLARITY Act resolves. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency owns the stablecoin issuer; the Commodity Futures Trading Commission owns the derivative markets where the cascade lands; and a depegged stablecoin may simultaneously fall under the Securities and Exchange Commission's jurisdiction as a potential investment contract under the Howey test. No statute allocates liability or mandates coordination among these three agencies when the transmission crosses their respective boundaries, and no mechanism exists for assigning jurisdictional primacy before all three assert competing claims. DAO governance failure compounds the problem by creating a distinct transmission mechanism operating at blockchain speed, with no identifiable counterparty and no circuit breaker. This Article argues that closing the crosstagion gap requires not new prudential requirements but a designated tri-agency coordination mechanism, triggered by observable stress indicators, that assigns jurisdictional primacy and activates a classification standstill before a crisis rather than after.

detail.abstract: This study points out a thematic analysis of political corruption in West Bengal from 2010 to 2020, a decade of scandals and scams from the 34-year Left Front (CPI-M) regime to the All India Trinamool Congress (TMC) administration. This research maps the evolution of corruption from an institutionalised, party-centric model to a more personalised, transactional, and populist form. Based on a qualitative research method and through analysis of major scandals, including the Saradha and Rose Valley Ponzi schemes, the Narada sting operation, and systemic rackets in illegal coal mining and cattle smuggling. The main research question of this study is: During the big political shift in West Bengal from 2010 to 2020, what did corruption by politicians actually look like, what were the most common types of scams, and how exactly did they execute them? The main objectives of this study are 1) to systematically document and classify the major incidents of political corruption reported in West Bengal between 2010 and 2020. 2) To find out the various impacts of corruption on West Bengal's governance, economic development, public trust, and political landscape. The main findings of this study are: 1) the political economy of dejection, where socio-economic numbness created easy ground for fraudulent financial schemes that expanded on political guardianship. 2) The normalisation of corruption, where the TMC's populist welfarism created a public perception of bribery as a "necessary evil" for accessing state services, and a disconnect between corruption allegations and electoral outcomes. In conclusion, the corrupt system and untrustworthy political parties signify an undemocratic and petty way of politics in West Bengal.

title: The Wrong Plaintiff: Contract Damages versus Network Expulsion and the Collapse of Distributed Governance
affiliations: University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law

detail.title: The Wrong Plaintiff: Contract Damages versus Network Expulsion and the Collapse of Distributed Governance
detail.abstract:
Courts awarding standard contract remedies can destroy private network governance. In collectively governed trading networks, commercial cooperation often depends on the credible threat of ostracism. That threat is best understood as a club good: excludable because only members benefit from the network’s ability to sanction rule-breakers, and nonrivalrous because one member’s benefit from that enforcement capacity does not diminish another’s. Indeed, the threat often exhibits positive network effects: the larger the network, the greater the cost of exclusion and the stronger the deterrent.

Yet courts sometimes undermine a network’s power to ostracize by applying a doctrinal framework that identifies only the individual promisee as the injured party. When judicial intervention displaces the network’s authority to exclude violators, it converts collective exclusion from a property rule into a liability rule and degrades the club good into a public good. Making one obligee whole through expectation damages can therefore produce a net welfare loss by weakening the credibility of exclusion. A court’s effort to remedy a single breach may thus eliminate the incentive to maintain the network itself. Courts must recognize this mechanism to avoid collapsing valuable transactional networks.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a condition-based approach to assessing institutional stability in advanced governance systems. It argues that institutions operating under sustained uncertainty exhibit identifiable patterns of systemic strain that affect decision behavior long before observable performance decline or formal malfunction. Rather than relying on crisis indicators, output metrics, or retrospective failure analysis, the paper focuses on adaptive capacity as the ability of decision systems to sustain responsibility-bearing action under cognitive and procedural load. By examining changes in decision latency, responsibility perception, and procedural mediation, the paper proposes an analytical framework for measuring institutional condition without normative judgment or reform agendas. The contribution lies in providing a diagnostic perspective suitable for institutional self-observation, regulatory reflection, and long-term resilience assessment.

title: Exclusive Inclusion: How University Governance Produces the Discrimination It Promises to Prevent

detail.title: Exclusive Inclusion: How University Governance Produces the Discrimination It Promises to Prevent
detail.abstract: Institutions publicly committed to "inclusive" can produce systematic identity-based exclusion as a structural output. This Essay introduces exclusive inclusion to name this condition: the governance state in which self-perpetuating boards, unenforceable fiduciary duties, and the absence of stakeholder standing create an accountability void that organized factions exploit to exclude disfavored identity groups. The mechanism is architectural, not attitudinal, and operates across identity categories: Women of Color in STEM, Black students at liberal arts colleges, conservative faculty, Jewish students, and students with disabilities all face exclusion through the same governance failures. Drawing on organizational theory and the author's prior work on "sovereign charities," this Essay offers a diagnostic tool, the disentanglement matrix, to separate protected individual expression from institutional identitybased exclusion. Three structural reforms follow: stakeholder standing modeled on corporate derivative suits, enforceable mission specificity, and an operational test for tax exemption adapted from hospital community benefit standards. Because exclusive inclusion is structural, governance reform benefits every affected constituency.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming organizational decision-making, workforce structure, and operational workflows. However, its implementation introduces fundamental contradictions that challenge traditional management models. This paper develops a conceptual framework identifying nine core organizational contradictions arising from AI integration, including autonomy versus human oversight, efficiency versus trust, bias mitigation versus bias amplification, job displacement versus augmentation, and innovation speed versus governance stability. Drawing on empirical evidence from industry case studies, regulatory developments, and organizational research, the analysis demonstrates that AI is neither purely an automation tool nor purely an augmentation tool, but an organizational forcing function that reshapes the cognitive and structural architecture of work. The findings suggest that organizations treating AI as a plug-and-play efficiency tool often experience degraded trust, deskilling, and operational fragility, while organizations that redesign workflows, governance systems, and leadership roles around human-AI collaboration achieve sustainable performance gains. This paper introduces the concept of the "AI-native organization," defined as an organization structurally redesigned to integrate AI as an amplifier of human judgment rather than a replacement for human capability. The framework contributes to the emerging literature on AI governance, human-AI collaboration, and organizational transformation by providing a structured model for understanding the paradoxical effects of AI implementation.

title: Contingent Enforcement and the Endogenous Limits of Firm Scale

detail.title: Contingent Enforcement and the Endogenous Limits of Firm Scale
detail.abstract: This paper develops a firm-level framework showing how contingent enforcement constrains firm scale and shapes organizational form. In many institutional environments, legal rules exist, but enforcement is episodic rather than continuously binding. Standard models explain regulatory risk through detection probability or output-proportional penalties. This paper instead identifies a distinct structural channel: the conditional cost imposed when enforcement is activated. As firms expand, fixed commitments, organizational coupling, and reduced reversibility may cause regulatory intervention to affect a larger share of productive activity. When enforcement exposure rises faster than buffering capacity, the marginal conditional enforcement cost increases with scale. Even if enforcement probability remains constant, this mechanism endogenously limits firm growth. The model formalizes this trade-off and derives implications for organizational segmentation, firm size distributions, and cross-jurisdictional variation under contingent enforcement. By isolating scale-dependent conditional disruption-distinct from detection-based models-the paper advances institutional and development economics and lays the groundwork for empirical analysis of firm behavior under episodic enforcement.

detail.abstract: This paper analyses the efficiency of employment subsidies versus job retention schemes in a random search-and-matching model with human capital depreciation during unemployment and endogenous job destruction. Unlike under exogenous destruction, employment subsidies aimed at correcting inefficient hiring now distort the job-destruction margin, resulting in excess job destruction and turnover. title: System-Level Security as Institutional Capital: Expanding Feasible Economic Action Sets

detail.title: System-Level Security as Institutional Capital: Expanding Feasible Economic Action Sets
detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural framework in which system-level security determines the admissibility of economic action classes. Rather than modeling insecurity as a marginal distortion to expected returns, the analysis treats protection against force-backed coercion as a feasibility constraint. Economic actions are feasible only when exposure implies a sufficiently high probability of unrecoverable loss exceeding actors' buffers. When this threshold is crossed, actions become infeasible regardless of expected profitability. Security is defined functionally as the stability of broadly accessible expectations regarding protection against coercive loss and the recoverability of such loss within economically relevant horizons. Improvements in system-level security expand the feasible action correspondence, while deterioration contracts it. These shifts occur along structural margins that scale exposure, including time horizon, geographic reach, and relational scope. Transactions characterized by high irreversibility, long duration, broad geographic scope, or impersonal exchange are especially sensitive to changes in security conditions. The framework generates nonlinear and heterogeneous predictions, including threshold effects, buffer-conditioned responses, and structural segmentation when stability is confined to specific domains rather than widely accessible. These mechanisms imply observable shifts in contract duration, geographic integration, capital commitment, and impersonal exchange as security conditions change. The paper contributes a feasibility-based security framework that yields threshold, heterogeneity, and ordered contraction predictions for economic structure.

title: Geopolitical Risk, Financial Sanctions, and Corporate Credit Risk: Payment Feasibility Risk in the Global Financial System

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk, Financial Sanctions, and Corporate Credit Risk: Payment Feasibility Risk in the Global Financial System
detail.abstract: Recent geopolitical developments have exposed structural limitations in traditional models of corporate credit analysis. Financial solvency, long considered the primary determinant of a firm's ability to honour its obligations, has proven insufficient in an environment where geopolitical decisions can disrupt the financial infrastructure that enables international payments. This paper examines how geopolitical risk-particularly economic and financial sanctionsaffects the operational capacity of firms to execute cross-border transactions. Drawing on recent evidence from the sanctions imposed following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the analysis highlights the distinction between insolvency-driven default and operational payment disruption. Building on insights from international political economy and the structure of the international financial system, the paper proposes an analytical framework for integrating geopolitical risk into corporate credit assessment. The framework combines geopolitical monitoring, exposure mapping, and stress-testing mechanisms designed to anticipate disruptions in global financial networks. An illustrative scenario involving a Brazilian financial institution demonstrates how the proposed approach could mitigate exposure to geopolitical payment disruptions. The findings suggest that integrating geopolitical variables into credit analysis can significantly improve the resilience of financial institutions operating in an increasingly politicised global financial system.

detail.abstract: Understanding how experience shapes promotion to managerial roles is of central interest to both organizations and employees. Prior research offers competing views on whether advancement favors skill specialization or broader experience, yet provides limited insight into how organizations evaluate these dimensions when making promotion decisions. Drawing on a signaling perspective, we examine how specialization relative to a promotion job and accumulated skill variety function as distinct but partially overlapping signals of promotability. Using personnel records and job descriptions from a large international pharmaceutical company, we analyze 28,699 candidate-job observations involving 1,104 employees considered for promotion to 117 managerial positions over four years. We find that both specialization and skill variety independently increase promotion chances, but in a less-than-additive manner, such that each can compensate for the other. We further show that the informational value of these signals varies with job characteristics and relational context, including social capital. These findings advance a phenomenon-based understanding of promotion decisions and inform debates on specialization, experience variety, and talent management in contemporary internal labor markets.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that agentic artificial intelligence represents a structural transformation distinct from prior waves of automation and even earlier general-purpose technologies. Unlike generative systems that augment individual tasks, agentic AI performs goal decomposition, tool selection, multi-step execution, and autonomous coordination across workflows. We introduce the concept of Coordination Infrastructure Technology (CIT) to characterize agentic AI as a technology that reduces coordination costs at scale. Building on institutional economics, the paper develops the Coordination Compression Hypothesis (CCH) and the Dynamic Agentic Productivity Gradient (DAPG) to explain how agentic systems reshape firm boundaries, capital allocation, labor stratification, and national economic divergence. We argue that economies with higher AI orchestration capacity accumulate intangible capital faster and capture greater digital rents, while AI-consuming economies risk structural dependency. Through conceptual modeling, comparative institutional analysis, and long-horizon scenario mapping, the paper outlines implications for development strategy, platform capitalism, and governance capacity. The findings suggest that agentic AI may function not merely as a productivity-enhancing tool, but as a coordination-layer infrastructure technology capable of reconfiguring global economic hierarchies.

detail.abstract: Do aggressive, hyper-competitive workplace cultures drive success, or undermine it? Although such cultures appear across a wide range of industries, from tech and consulting to academia, their link to workplace performance remains largely unexamined. Drawing on survey and archival data from over 1,000 faculty and staff across five European business schools, we measure individual perceptions of masculinity contest culture (MCC) and construct novel indicators of shared beliefs at the reference group level. We find that MCC is consistently associated with lower employee well-being and higher turnover intentions. Critically, we find no positive associations with academics' publication rates or citation impact, and instead observe reduced overall research output. Both men and women show negative associations between MCC, well-being and productivity, with no advantages even for star performers. However, women experience additional citation penalties, indicating that MCC may exacerbate gender disparities in how research is evaluated. These findings challenge common assumptions that aggressively competitive cultures are necessary for research excellence. "I think a lot of the corporate world is pretty culturally neutered. Masculine energy is good, and obviously, society has plenty of that, but I think corporate culture was really trying to get away from it. I think having a culture that celebrates the aggression a bit more has its own merits that are really positive."

detail.abstract: Since 2018, tariffs have re-emerged as a tool for protecting domestic economies, particularly in the US. This paper examines the macroeconomic and welfare effects of various import tariff scenarios using a four-region dynamic general equilibrium model with a multi-sectoral production network. The scenarios include unilateral US tariffs, coordinated US-EU tariffs, Chinese retaliation, Europe’s non-participation, and sector-specific versus broad tariffs. Our results show that tariffs initially boost domestic value-added output by making local goods relatively cheaper. While consumption can increase permanently, the output benefits are short-lived. Increased production costs and reduced global income largely offset the output gains over time. Tariff-targeted countries have an incentive to retaliate, and when they do, these output/consumption gains do not materialize. As a result, welfare effects are negative. Regardless of direct involvement in tariff conflicts, the rest of the world suffers from reduced aggregate income. The effects of tariffs and strategic interactions depend on which sectors are subject to tariffs. Overall, tariffs appear to be an inefficient tool for economic protection due to the high probability of retaliation.

title: Dual-Buffer Straddle Strategy: How Fill Rates Reveal the Distinct Roles of Execution Design and Ensemble-Based Machine Learning Prediction

detail.title: Dual-Buffer Straddle Strategy: How Fill Rates Reveal the Distinct Roles of Execution Design and Ensemble-Based Machine Learning Prediction
detail.abstract: We extend the buffer-based limit order execution framework for machine learning trading strategies by introducing a dual-buffer mechanism that applies patient limit order exits to both legs of a straddle position. Building upon the single-buffer "patient trader" approach—where only the losing leg exits via limit orders—our enhancement captures additional profit from the winning position through symmetric execution at favorable prices.Testing three ML algorithms (XGBoost, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) across 48 global securities over 1,989 trading days (2018–2025) with buffer levels from 10% to 40%, we find the dual-buffer approach dramatically outperforms the single-buffer methodology. At the 30% buffer level, the dual-buffer strategy achieves Sharpe ratios of 17.40 under full execution versus 3.17 for the original single-buffer approach. A fill rate degradation analysis—evaluating performance as the kept leg’s buffer execution probability decreases from 100% to 50%—demonstrates graceful degradation: at the 30% buffer, Sharpe ratios decline from 17.40 to 10.29, still exceeding the original methodology by a factor of three and buy-and-hold by a factor of seventeen. The original single-buffer results constitute the performance floor, achieved when the kept leg always closes at market. Comprehensive risk analysis using VaR, CVaR, and Maximum Drawdown confirms enhanced risk-adjusted performance across all fill rate assumptions.Robustness analyses across five subperiods—including the COVID-19 crisis—demonstrate strategy stability, with Deflated Sharpe Ratios confirming significance after adjusting for 576 strategy configurations. Our findings demonstrate that the dual-buffer mechanism generates substantial execution alpha under full buffer execution independent of prediction quality, while ML prediction’s directional accuracy becomes the critical floor-preserving mechanism as kept-leg fill rates degrade.

detail.abstract: Organizations frequently invest in artificial intelligence yet struggle to convert early experimentation into durable behavioral change. This paper offers a conceptual framework for diagnosing that problem. It argues that sustained adoption in organizational systems can be analyzed through three broad conditions: the internal state of the individual, the social environment that signals what behavior is modeled and socially permitted, and the structural context that either supports or penalizes repeated use. Rather than competing with established theories of behavior, technology acceptance, or organizational learning, the paper synthesizes them into a parsimonious, intervention-oriented classification intended to clarify why some change efforts stall despite competent execution. The article draws on prior research on identity, psychological safety, trust in automation, social learning, leadership signaling, workflow design, learning infrastructure, and measurement, and shows how these elements map onto the WHEEL framework introduced in prior work. The paper is conceptual and theory-building in scope. It does not present new empirical estimates. Instead, it develops a compact diagnostic structure, practical implications for intervention sequencing, and several propositions for future empirical research on organizational adoption, persistence, and AI readiness.

detail.abstract: This paper makes three original contributions to the governance of artificial intelligence systems in regulated enterprise environments. First, it establishes that board-level accountability under deployer frameworks, particularly as formalized in the EU AI Act, constitutes a fiduciary obligation structurally equivalent to credit, operational, and cyber risk oversight, requiring the same formal integration into enterprise risk management. Second, it introduces authority drift as a first-class enterprise risk variable: the condition by which delegated autonomy in agentic AI systems expands in scope, duration, or privilege concentration without formal reclassification or appetite review, producing material governance exposure that traditional control environments are not designed to detect. Third, it presents the first unified governance loop connecting model risk governance [1] and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework [2] to the governance of delegated authority in agentic systems demonstrating that Continuous Governance [3] is the operating norm capable of spanning both architecture types without requiring a new governance philosophy. The paper develops an autonomy tiering framework classifying AI systems from advisory outputs (Tier 0) to material consequence authority (Tier 4), an enterprise risk management integration model including appetite cascade and residual risk aggregation, structural mechanisms for escalation under ambiguity, architectural containment of delegated authority, and enterprise-level visibility requirements for board oversight. Together these form a governance architecture defensible under regulatory examination, board scrutiny, and operational pressure.

detail.abstract: Societies function as complex adaptive systems, continually absorbing changes across economic, cultural, technological, demographic, and political dimensions. A critical yet underexamined factor in this process is the tempo at which change enters the system and is cognitively integrated by individuals and social structures. This paper presents a conceptual framework linking electoral institutions to the rhythm of societal adaptation (Lijphart, 1999), contrasting high-volatility and absorptive systems. Using comparative observations of the United States and Denmark, it argues that concentrated authority accelerates political and social recalibration, producing abrupt cognitive and social adaptation cycles, whereas distributed authority facilitates gradual integration, supporting stability and continuity. By situating this analysis within systems thinking and cognitive observation, the paper foregrounds the experiential and perceptual dimensions of governance. It contributes a theoretical lens for understanding how institutional design shapes the pace at which societies absorb change and highlights avenues for future empirical investigation into the interplay between electoral structure, social networks, and collective cognition.

detail.title: A Methodological Integration of MCDA and Visual Governance Tools: Evidence-Weighted Value–Viability Assessment
detail.abstract: This study addresses limitations of fully compensatory multi-criteria prioritisation by proposing an evidence-weighted, bi-dimensional framework that separates Value (expected public or strategic benefit) from Viability (delivery readiness). By reducing complex MCDA outputs to two governance-relevant dimensions, the approach enhances visual interpretation, supports decisionmakers with predominantly managerial profiles, and makes non-compensatory trade-offs explicit. Globally validated Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) weights are used to aggregate raw 1–5 ratings, mapped to a monotone-better scale, into two composite indices (Value and Viability). Proposals are positioned on a governance-oriented 3×3 matrix using tertile thresholds (33rd/67th percentiles) on each axis. The four corner cells (Low×Low, High×Low, Low×High, and High×High) are associated with prescriptive governance actions, cells containing exactly one Medium category are treated as transition bands, and the central Medium×Medium cell is interpreted as a zone of managerial flexibility. New proposals can be incorporated incrementally by scoring and plotting themwithout re-running the entire portfolio. A fully reproducible R workflow computes composite scores and generates the visual outputs. In an illustrative application using a simulated public-healthportfolio (n=39), the bivariate representation reveals Value–Viability imbalances that are masked by single-index rankings. The framework limits compensatory masking, highlights delivery constraints affecting high-value initiatives, and makes explicit when feasible but lower-value proposals may remain attractive under available capacity, while preserving expert-elicited trade-offs within each dimension. Overall, the study bridges managerial visual matrices and MCDA rigor by delivering an auditable, evidence-weighted prioritisation instrument that combines dimensional reduction, visual governance, explicit non-compensatory safeguards, and incremental portfolio extensibility, supported by an open R script implementation.

detail.abstract: The repeated withdrawal of the U.S. from the Paris Agreement points to a broader Trumpian shock to global governance, in which domestic populism and executive-driven policy reversals destabilise international cooperation. This commentary examines how U.S. political volatility interacts with global power asymmetries to weaken institutional trust and reshape collective climate action. Drawing on realism and liberalism as interpretive perspectives, the analysis traces the systemic effects of U.S. withdrawal across climate diplomacy, climate finance, the energy transition, and economic productivity and public health. detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across organizational information systems has fundamentally altered how information and knowledge are produced, circulated, and consumed. Large language models and related generative architectures are increasingly embedded in decision support systems, enterprise platforms, and public-sector infrastructures, where their outputs inform operational, strategic, and policy decisions. While prior research has primarily conceptualized GenAI as an enabling technology that augments human cognition, productivity, and creativity, it has largely treated GenAI outputs as conventional information or knowledge artifacts. This assumption overlooks a critical system-level transformation introduced by generative systems: the large-scale production of synthetic knowledge whose epistemic properties differ materially from human-generated or empirically grounded organizational knowledge. To address this gap, this paper develops a systemlevel synthesis of the emerging GenAI literature and introduces synthetic knowledge as a distinct class of AI-generated epistemic artifacts. Drawing on established frameworks in information quality, decision support systems, trust and automation bias, and information systems governance, we conceptualize synthetic knowledge as probabilistically generated, weakly grounded, and recursively reused across socio-technical systems. We formalize synthetic knowledge using analytical abstractions and propose lifecycle and trust-calibration models suitable for engineering analysis and intelligent system design. Building on this synthesis, the paper derives concrete design and governance implications for managing synthetic knowledge in GenAI-enabled systems, emphasizing provenance-aware architectures, auditability-by-design, and lifecycle-sensitive risk controls. The paper concludes by outlining a multi-level research agenda that positions synthetic knowledge as a foundational construct for the design, evaluation, and governance of intelligent systems operating in the generative AI era.

detail.abstract:
Over the past two decades, businesses hiring across borders have increasingly turned to third-party intermediaries to handle the legal and administrative complexity of employing people in other countries. 

Four categories of service now dominate this market: Employer of Record (EOR), Professional Employer Organization (PEO), Global Payroll, and Contractor of Record (COR). The problem is that all four terms get used interchangeably, by vendors, advisors, and sometimes regulators, despite describing arrangements with meaningfully different legal structures, use cases, and risk profiles. 

This paper proposes a formal taxonomy to distinguish the four. Drawing on regulatory definitions, the International Labour Organization's (ILO) framework for employment relationships, academic literature on platform work and worker classification, and over a decade of direct observation in the global employment solutions market, the taxonomy is built around four dimensions: (1) legal employer or engagement status, (2) entity requirement, (3) jurisdictional portability, and (4) co-employment or shared-liability structure. 

A practitioner decision framework is also offered. This is a conceptual paper. Testing the taxonomy empirically across jurisdictions is beyond the scope of this work and is an explicit priority for future research.

detail.abstract: Rapid growth in e-commerce has dramatically increased home delivery activity in cities, intensifying the movement of goods and the associated economic, social, and environmental impacts. Coordinating deliveries across multiple logistics providers has the potential to improve efficiency and societal outcomes, but doing so requires mechanisms that can match delivery demand with heterogeneous service providers while accounting for customer preferences and operational costs. Motivated by this challenge, we study a matching problem in which a central decision maker, referred to as an independent market operator, allocates last-mile parcel deliveries among competing providers with the goal of enhancing public value. Customers value service attributes such as price, service quality, and environmental performance, while providers incur scale-dependent operating costs. We show that Nash equilibria exist but are generally not unique. We develop a constructive procedure to establish the existence of a Nash equilibrium and show that it can be used as a solution method to identify optimal assignments under specific conditions. For more general cases, we propose a mixed-integer programming formulation with a clustering-based reduction that scales to instances with more than 2,500 customers. Numerical experiments show that decentralized behavior may lead the system to substantially different equilibrium outcomes, with welfare gaps exceeding 20% across equilibria for the problem instances we study. Centralized assignments by the independent market operator ensure selection of the highest-value equilibrium, which our experiments show typically lies on the environmental-quality efficient frontier, indicating that improvements in societal utility can be achieved without significant sacrifices in these dimensions.

detail.abstract:
The American Law Institute’s Corporate Governance Project is one of the most comprehensive and controversial attempts to “modernize” American corporate law. Much of the controversy surrounding the Project is undoubtedly due to its authors’ bold attempt to change various established doctrines of corporate law rather than merely restate them. One of the controversial reforms originally proposed by the Project involved changes in the structure and composition of corporate boards of directors. 

In a recent article, we called into question the need, efficacy and shareholder welfare consequences of mandatory changes in the composition of corporate boards of directors as proposed by the American Law Institute (ALI). Our approach, in a nutshell, was to suggest conceptually and demonstrate empirically that corporate managements, in response to a variety of institutional pressures, have facilitated the evolution of efficient governance structures. We concluded that such evolutionary changes eliminated the need for the imposition of mandatory structural reforms. In a critique of our research appearing in the same symposium issue, Professor Melvin Eisenberg—the Chief Reporter on the Project and a long-time advocate of corporate changes—implied that a nutshell was the appropriate container for this conclusion. We naturally disagree with the substance of this assessment and find revealed in the very nature of its presentation a more transcendent issue that should be aired.

A careful review of Professor Eisenberg’s “New Modes of Discourse” suggests to us that Professor Eisenberg's goal was not merely to point out what he perceived as conceptual and methodological errors in our research design, as is standard practice in the process of scientific research. Rather, the goal apparently was the larger one of proving that the scientific method is a “new mode of discourse,” and one that should not be allowed to intrude on the traditional style of discourse familiar to legal scholars. In many respects this is simply an attack on the propriety of the type of authentication process employed by “law and economics” scholars. Unfortunately, his critique contains so many conceptual errors and misrepresentations of the economic theory of the corporation that it cannot be more than a catalyst to a debate among others about the appropriate methodology in analyzing corporate law proposals. Moreover, it is entirely insensitive to the reasonableness requirements of empirical science.

The purpose of this article is to present a detailed rebuttal to Professor Eisenberg’s attack on our scholarship. Section I discusses the value of quantitative research as a guide to public policy and responds to Professor Eisenberg's attack on the quality of our empirical work. A major point of this section is that his “old” mode of discourse does not contain any mechanisms designed to explicitly identify the relevant trade-offs involved in the implementation of public policies. Section II presents a detailed rebuttal of Professor Eisenberg’s critique of our conceptual analysis. A careful reading of Professor Eisenberg’s comments suggests that he has not captured the subtleties of many of the recent developments in the economic theory of the corporation. In Section III, we respond to Professor Eisenberg’s claim that our research is politically motivated. While our research is conservative in the tradition of positive economic science, it is certainly not politically motivated. The final section presents some concluding comments.

detail.abstract:
Are we on the precipice of developing autonomous killer robots; unmanned technologies that will completely dominate conflict, remorselessly, perfectly? Some advocates think so but this article explains why the "killer robot" focus is misdirected: it draws attention away from how militaries already use artificial intelligence technologies. 

Drawing upon operational constraints, technological capabilities, legal frameworks, and military culture, this Article demonstrates that autonomous "killer robots" are neither the aspiration nor the trajectory of military AI development. Instead, by centering the targeting process, a dimension almost entirely overlooked in existing literature, this Article reveals that militaries deploy AI not to eliminate human judgment but to enhance it across multiple decision-making stages: studying adversaries, managing escalation risks, and reducing civilian casualties through intelligence analysis and target verification. The killer robot narrative drives policy responses aimed at banning technologies that don't exist while ignoring the systems already shaping warfare. With a clearer understanding, this Article identifies meliorative opportunities that address the actual landscape of military AI rather than science fiction scenarios.

detail.abstract:
By the 1970s, a nearly unanimous Antitrust community had concluded that the Federal Trade Commission‘s (FTC) enforcement of the Robinson-Patman Act perverted Antitrust law. FTC enforcement declined and then was abandoned entirely, with the Supreme Court declaring in 2006 that lower courts should avoid applying Robinson Patman in ways “geared more to the protection of existing competitors than to the stimulation of competition.” Shattering this consensus, the Biden FTC brought the first two government cases in many years (one continued by the Trump FTC). The Biden Commissioners claimed that the old consensus both misunderstood the nature of the statute and was based on faulty reasoning of the Chicago school and the Reagan Administration. 

The revivalist story of Robinson Patman’s history is fictitious, denying the statute’s protectionist origins. Only 15 days after the Supreme Court struck down the government’s attempt to end the Great Depression by cartelizing business to raise prices, Wright Patman introduced “The Wholesaler Grocer’s Protection Act,” written by the wholesaler grocer trade association and seeking the same goal in a different guise. To overcome significant opposition, including from the Roosevelt Administration, the actual legislation included new defenses and greater complexity and ambiguity. The result was, as historian Ellis Hawley concluded, “a vague law,” the “actual effects of which would depend on its administration and interpretation.” Nevertheless, the FTC through the 1960s took an aggressive competitor-protection approach to enforcement. An overwhelming consensus developed that the Act was used to protect competitors rather than competition and consumers. Beginning in 1970, the FTC abandoned Robinson Patman as the center of its competition universe, long before the Reagan Administration. 

Surprisingly, revivalists also claim no evidence shows that Robinson Patman enforcement was anticompetitive, ignoring both business responses to the Act and the many studies of problematic FTC enforcement. This report for the Competitive Enterprise Institute details numerous, well-known examples of enforcement and policy that raised cost and reduced competition. For example, the FTC encouraged direct competitors to share their prices; it discouraged selective price cutting in industries most susceptible to tacit or explicit collusion; and it discouraged small businesses from cooperating to compete successfully with larger ones. The overwhelming experience of the businesses, attorneys, and others most exposed to Robinson Patman is compelling evidence that led them to revolt and conclude that FTC enforcement was fundamentally inconsistent with antitrust’s purpose of protecting competition and consumers.

Finally, in a companion piece summarized here, “Stop Making Sense: Reviving the Robinson-Patman Act, and the Economics of Intermediate Price Discrimination,“ SSRN-6299819, Bruce Kobayashi and I discuss current economic literature, both theoretical and empirical, regarding intermediate price discrimination. Economists continue to debunk the economic incoherence of a favorite argument of revivalists, used 90 years ago and resurrected today, that discounts to large retailers are only possible because small firms pay more. Modern theoretical justifications of mandating uniform pricing show beneficial results are possible, but only in narrow circumstances that provide no practical or policy guidance. Moreover, when key institutional features of pricing that large firms actually use are incorporated, the results support using, not restricting, differential pricing. Not surprisingly, empirical studies fail to support revival. Causal evidence of harm from intermediate price discrimination is nonexistent, and indirect evidence is consistent both with the benefits of differential pricing and the high costs of the efforts of the FTC and others to impose uniformity.

detail.abstract: This paper, The TRIPS Imbroglio: Challenges in Balancing Innovation and Access in a Globalising World, examines the complexities of the Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) agreement within the context of the World Trade Organization (WTO) legal order. The study explores how developing nations navigate the TRIPS framework, highlighting the challenges they encounter in reconciling the need to foster innovation with the imperative of ensuring equitable access to essential goods, such as pharmaceuticals and technology. By analysing the legal and policy interpretations of TRIPS provisions, the paper delves into the tensions between the protection of intellectual property rights and public health, as well as the broader economic and social implications for developing countries. It further investigates how differing interpretations of TRIPS, influenced by the WTO’s legal framework, have led to divergent outcomes in the Global South. Through a critical analysis, this paper offers insights into the difficulties faced by developing nations when balancing their obligations under TRIPS with the need to promote affordable access to vital innovations, highlighting the role of the WTO in shaping these debates in an increasingly globalised world.

Guzman, Ph.D, https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5946-9151, Yolly B. Dequito, MPA, Francisco III O. Baluyut, Blessy Ann L. Ayco This study examined the perceptions and institutional impacts of the 4-day Compressed Workweek (CWW) arrangement among university personnel (n=215). Utilizing a quantitative research design, the study analyzed demographic profiles, perceived advantages, and operational impacts through Chi-Square Tests for Independence and One-Way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). The workforce was predominantly female (64.2%) and comprised largely of permanent (48.4%) and Contract of Service (38.1%) employees. Findings indicate high policy acceptance, with 90.7% of respondents favoring the 4-day schedule. Statistical analysis revealed that perceived advantages primarily improved work-life balance (62.8%) and economic savings (60.9%) are universal, showing no significant relationship with gender or employment status (p > 0.05). However, a significant relationship exists between gender and Sense of Safety while Traveling (p = 0.037), with female personnel reporting lower safety perceptions (=3.88) due to late-hour commutes. Furthermore, physical and mental exhaustion (29.3%) emerged as the primary challenge. Recommendations include gender-responsive measures such as an institutional shuttle service and enhanced campus security. To mitigate fatigue and ensure five-day service continuity, the study proposes institutionalizing 15-minute wellness breaks and a staggered staffing rotation. These adjustments ensure the CWW remains a sustainable, inclusive, and efficient administrative model.

detail.abstract: Multi-agent coordination architectures are increasingly marketed as enabling scalable, parallel productivity through hierarchical orchestration. This paper analyzes a structural constraint on effective system velocity within a specific architecture class: hierarchical orchestration with partial output discard under uncertainty. Within a formally specified model interface, this paper models net velocity for an n-agent hierarchy with branching factor k, per-agent output capacity c, expected discard burden m, and convergence tolerance e as v(n) = cn-kn log k (n)-mne-4. This paper proves that the coordination drag term kn log k (n) is a structural lower bound under bounded fan-in hierarchies (Theorem 5.1), and models the discard term mne-4 as a modeled scaling regime within the stated interface (Model 5.2). Under the proved coordination drag bound (Theorem 5.1) combined with the modeled discard regime (Model 5.2), there exists a threshold n 0 beyond which v(n) decreases monotonically as n increases.

title: Topological Governance of Autonomous AI Agents in Regulated Financial Services: An Empirical Analysis with Network Contagion Modelling

detail.title: Topological Governance of Autonomous AI Agents in Regulated Financial Services: An Empirical Analysis with Network Contagion Modelling

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founding CEO of Meridian Autonomy, which builds governance intelligence infrastructure for financial institutions. The methodology described in this paper underpins the company's data architecture.

detail.abstract:
Between 2022 and 2025, financial institutions across Europe and North America began deploying AI as operational agents rather than analytical tools. This paper presents the first large-scale analysis of externally observable AI agent governance signals in global financial services, combined with a network contagion model for assessing cascading governance failure. Using a twenty-eight-dimension intelligence architecture across seven analytical layers, we constructed a structured dataset covering 795 financial institutions across 94 countries, identifying over 20,000 autonomous AI agents and mapping 105,402 typed dependency edges across eleven relationship categories.

Our methodology applies graph-theoretic topology to model governance as a network of relationships between agents, oversight structures, regulatory obligations, and data dependencies, rather than as a static inventory of assets. We introduce a network contagion model in which governance failure propagates through typed directional edges, with each edge type carrying a distinct contagion coefficient. The model also incorporates protective edges, where governance connections and halt mechanisms actively reduce an agent’s failure probability. This provides the first quantitative framework for measuring the value of governance infrastructure in agent networks.

The principal findings are consistent across the sampled population. 95% of AI agents across 104 deep-scanned institutions have no observable halt mechanism. Investment managers exhibit the weakest observable governance posture of any sector. Under the model assumptions, cascade simulation indicates that a single agent failure propagates through an average of 38 connected agents across four rounds of contagion, with worst-case blast radii exceeding 50 agents. Every institution in the deep-scanned sample has critical-materiality agents with zero observable protective governance edges.

We introduce three theoretical propositions grounding AI agent governance in network topology and transaction cost economics, and contribute a reproducible methodology for agent-level governance assessment, an empirical baseline for cross-institutional benchmarking, and a contagion framework that models governance as a dynamic network property rather than a static compliance attribute.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of sustainable e-marketing practices on consumer perceptions and purchasing behaviours among Indian online shoppers of eco-friendly products, within the framework of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 12. Using a crosssectional survey of 160 respondents, the research examines key factors including green awareness, perceived usefulness, and trust in e-commerce platforms, and their influence on purchase intention and actual sustainable buying behaviour. The findings reveal that all three factors significantly and positively affect purchase intention, which in turn strongly predicts sustainable buying behaviour. Additionally, trust in platforms exhibits both direct and indirect effects on sustainable purchases, highlighting its pivotal role in bridging the intention-behaviour gap. The study underscores the importance of transparent, trustworthy, and informative sustainable e-marketing strategies to effectively encourage eco-friendly consumption in the growing Indian digital marketplace. Practical implications for marketers, e-commerce platforms, and policymakers are discussed to promote responsible consumption and advance sustainable development.

title: When More Experience Is Not More Helpful: Evidence from Positive and Negative Reviews on Steam
affiliations: Northwestern University - Department of Operations, Northwestern University - Department of Managerial Economics and Decision Sciences (MEDS) and

detail.title: When More Experience Is Not More Helpful: Evidence from Positive and Negative Reviews on Steam
detail.abstract: As user reviews grow on online platforms, separating useful feedback from noise becomes operationally crucial for guiding consumers and for triaging feedback internally (e.g., for product learning and quality assurance). Yet the most direct indicator of review helpfulness-readers' votes-arrives later, so platforms must assess the expected helpfulness of new reviews based on cues available at submission. Many platforms display reviewer experience cues, but it is unclear how such experience translates into perceived review helpfulness and whether the relationship differs for positive versus negative reviews. Using 26.8 million video-game reviews on Steam, where reviews display reviewers' cumulative playtime and a binary verdict (recommend/not recommend), we aim to address this question by estimating models with rich controls and fixed effects. We find that experience predicts helpfulness in a non-monotonic way, with opposite curvature by review verdict: U-shaped for recommended reviews (i.e., reviews from low-and high-experience users receive more helpful votes than reviews from moderately experienced users) but inverted-U for not-recommended reviews (peaking at moderate experience). Observable cues (e.g., review length, product maturity) systematically moderate these patterns. Our findings offer clear guidance for review management: rather than treating experience as a uniform quality signal, platforms should interpret and weigh experience differently based on review verdict and observable context cues.

detail.abstract: Temporal focal points shape high-stakes economic outcomes. We investigate this proposition in the U.S. mortgage market by documenting novel within-month patterns in lending. Using confidential Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data, we show that applications arrive smoothly throughout the month, yet approximately half of all originations occur in the final week. The Black approval gap, 2.4 percentage points unexplained at the start of the month, narrows to zero by month’s end. Underperforming loan officers and high-turnover lending institutions amplify this convergence. Demand-side factors, such as borrower financial constraints, also increase end-of-month volume, but the sensitivity does not vary meaningfully by applicant group
